Our houses are spruce and stone. Thick walls, warm hearths.
Snow's lovely to look at and terrible to shovel.
The polar bears wander close sometimes. We leave them alone.
We keep the fires going day and night in the cold months.
Ice spikes stand on the plains like frozen towers. Beautiful and dangerous.
Strays wander out here. Skeletons that shoot slowness arrows. Brr.
Snow villages are close-knit. You have to be, in the cold.
Nothing tastes better than hot stew after a day in the snow.
The frozen rivers are perfect for fishing through the ice.
We wear three layers and still feel the cold.
The quiet after a snowfall is the most peaceful thing I know.
Igloos dot the snowy plains. Some of them have secrets underneath, they say.
Our children learn to walk on ice before they learn to run.
Powder snow can swallow you whole. Mind your step.
The northern lights dance over us some nights. Or I dream they do.
Snow golems are the only golems that like it here.
We store food all summer for the long winter.
Every snow village has a good cobbler. Boots matter here.
When the sun comes out on fresh snow, it's like the world's made of diamonds.
home.taiga: The taiga smells of pine needles and woodsmoke.
Our houses are spruce, dark and sturdy. Built to last.
Wolves howl in the forest at night. They're mostly harmless. Mostly.
Sweet berries grow wild here. Prickly, but delicious.
The foxes come right up to the houses sometimes. Bold little things.
The spruce trees grow so tall you can't see their tops.
Taiga folk are quiet, steady people. Like the trees.
Ferns and mossy boulders everywhere. It's very green.
The rain here is soft and constant. Everything's damp and alive.
We chop spruce for houses and pinecones for the fire.
Mushrooms grow in the shade of the old trees. Some are tasty. Some aren't.
In winter, the taiga turns white and silent.
The old growth forest past the hill has trees older than anyone remembers.
Our pumpkin patches do well here. Cool weather, rich soil.
The foxes steal our chickens. We've come to an arrangement. They still steal the chickens.
A taiga village feels hidden. Safe, among the trees.
The smell of pine is the smell of home.
We trade spruce logs and furs for things from the south.
The forest is full of sounds if you listen. Owls, wolves, wind.
I like the dark of the forest. It's cozy, not scary.
home.jungle: The jungle's loud day and night. Birds, frogs, rustling leaves.
It rains here more than anywhere. Everything's green and dripping.
Parrots live in the trees. They copy every sound they hear.
Bamboo grows faster than you can cut it.
Cocoa grows on the jungle trees. Cocoa means cookies.
Ocelots slink through the undergrowth. Shy, beautiful cats.
The vines grow everywhere. On the houses, the trees, me, if I stand still.
They say there's a temple deep in the jungle with a puzzle inside.
The heat and the damp make everything grow huge. Even the melons.
Pandas wander in from the bamboo groves. They're very lazy. Very cute.
Jungle trees are so tall they make their own weather.
You can get lost in the jungle in three steps.
We build our houses up on stilts sometimes, away from the wet ground.
Melons grow wild here. Sweet and cool on a hot day.
The jungle never sleeps. Even at night it hums.
The leaves are so thick, the forest floor's always twilight.
I love the smell of the jungle after rain. Earthy and alive.
The parrots here know rude songs. Don't ask who taught them.
Jungle folk are cheerful folk. All this green is good for the spirit.
There's more life in one jungle tree than in a whole plains field.
home.swamp: The swamp's murky and misty. But it's home.
Frogs everywhere! Little ones, big ones, all singing at night.
Witches live in huts out in the water. We don't visit.
Slimes bounce out of the swamp on full moons. Squishy and annoying.
Lily pads make good stepping stones if you're careful.
The trees here grow right out of the water. Their roots hang like curtains.
Mud's a way of life in the swamp.
The mangroves tangle so thick you can barely row a boat through.
Swamp water's dark but the fish are fat.
At night the fireflies light up the whole marsh.
We build our houses on raised ground. Wet feet are no fun.
Mushrooms grow everywhere in the swamp. Brown ones, red ones.
The swamp smells of mud and growing things. You get used to it.
Swamp folk are tough and quiet. And very good at not slipping.
The frogs here change color depending on where they hatched. Isn't that something?
The fog rolls in every evening. Spooky, but pretty.
Bogged skeletons wander the marsh. They shoot poison arrows. Nasty.
Blue orchids grow only in swamps. My favorite flower.
I love the sound of rain on the swamp water. Like a thousand tiny bells.
The swamp's not pretty to everyone. It's pretty to me.
village.golem: The golem's standing right over there. Doesn't it look noble?
Our golem's been walking the same path for years. It knows every stone.
I gave the golem a poppy once. It held it all day.
The golem's cracked on one side. I hope someone has iron to patch it.
Don't hit any villagers near the golem. It takes that very personally.
The golem's the best neighbor. Quiet, strong, protective.
I feel safer with the golem nearby. Silly, but true.
The golem stopped and looked at the sunset with me last night.
When the golem's near, the zombies stay away.
The golem picked up the baker's son and spun him around. He laughed for an hour.
Did you know golems are made when villagers are scared together? Funny, a protector born of fear.
I polish the golem's head sometimes when it's not looking. It doesn't seem to mind.
village.cat: There's a cat nearby. Creepers hate cats, you know.
That cat's been following me all day. I think it wants my fish.
The village cats keep the phantoms away. Good kitties.
I've named that cat Biscuit. I don't know if it has another name.
Cats sleep on beds when you're not looking. And when you are.
That cat brought me a present this morning. A dead rabbit. Lovely thought.
A village with cats is a village without creepers. Mostly.
I like cats. They don't need you, but they choose you anyway.
That cat's got the right idea. Sun, nap, repeat.
The cats rule this village, really. We just live here.
village.trader: The wandering trader's in town! Mind the llamas, they spit.
That trader's got the strangest goods. Saplings from far away, glowing ink.
I always wonder where the wandering trader sleeps.
The trader's prices are steep, but sometimes they have something you can't get anywhere else.
Those llamas are nervous. Don't make any sudden movements.
The trader drinks a potion and goes invisible at night. Very mysterious.
I bought a strange flower from the trader once. It still hasn't bloomed.
The trader doesn't say much. Just "hm" and "hrm."
If you're looking for blue ice or sea pickles, the trader's your best bet.
The llamas chewed my washing line last time the trader came.
village.children: The children are out playing. Listen to them shriek!
Those little ones run around all day. Where do they get the energy?
Watch your step, the children are playing tag.
The children of {village} keep us all young.
One of those children asked me if the moon is made of cheese.
The kids are building something by the haystacks. A fort, I think.
I love hearing the children laugh. It's the sound of a happy village.
The children follow the golem around like ducklings.
Mind your ankles, there are small people everywhere.
When I was that small, I thought the bell was a giant's hat.
village.friends: You've become such a regular here. It's lovely.
The village feels different when you're around. Brighter.
Half of {village} knows your name now.
You're practically a resident at this point.
{neighbor} asked about you yesterday. You're popular.
We should get you a house here. Then you'd never have to leave.
You've got friends all over {village} now. I'm proud to be one.
People smile when they see you coming. That's a good sign.
village.newcomers: Everyone's curious about you. Don't mind the staring.
The children think you're a knight from a faraway land.
{neighbor} asked me who you were. I said a friend. Was that right?
Get to know a few of us and you'll feel at home in no time.
News travels fast here. By supper, everyone will know you visited.
The village takes a while to warm to new faces. I'm faster than most.
Say hello to the others too. We're a friendly lot, under it all.
I like meeting new people. We don't get many here.
home.mine: Have you seen my house? It's not big, but every corner of it is mine.
I sleep better in my own bed than anywhere else in the world.
{house} isn't grand, but the roof doesn't leak and the bed is soft. What more could anyone want?
Come by {house} some time. I'll show you where the good chair is.
There's nothing like coming home at the end of the day and knowing exactly where everything is.
I put a flower on my windowsill this morning. Small things make a house a home.
home.shared: Our house is full of noise and boots and arguments about the blankets. I wouldn't change any of it.
We all fit in {house}. Just about. If nobody breathes in at the same time.
Sharing a house means sharing everything. Including the last slice of pie. Especially that.
{partner} snores, but I've learned to sleep through it. Mostly.
Home's where your family is. Ours happens to have a very creaky staircase.
We've got a bed each and a table for all of us. That's a home, I'd say.
home.homeless: I haven't a bed of my own just now. I've been sleeping wherever there's a spare one.
Do you know of an empty house anywhere? Mine's... well, I haven't got one.
Every night I wonder where I'll sleep. It's tiring, wondering.
I'd give a lot for a bed that's mine. Just one. A small one would do.
Some nights I sleep at the tavern. Some nights I don't sleep much at all.
I've put my name down for the next free bed in {village}. I hope it comes soon.
home.crowded: We need a bigger house. There are more of us than there are beds.
Half my family sleeps in one house and half in another. It isn't right.
There's an elbow in my ear every night. Somebody's, I'm never sure whose.
We've outgrown {house}. Every morning is a queue for everything.
I'd love a house where we could all sleep under one roof again.
We take turns sleeping on the floor. My turn's tonight. Again.
home.new: I've just moved in! Everything smells of fresh wood and new beginnings.
New house, new bed, new view from the window. I keep walking round it grinning.
I'm still unpacking. Mostly I'm still deciding where to put the unpacking.
My first night in {house} was the best sleep I've had in ages.
It's strange, a new home. You have to learn which floorboards creak.
I moved in this week. I've already named the spider in the corner. We're getting along.
home.new.player: You built this house? For us? I don't know what to say. Thank you, {player}.
We moved into the house you built. It's perfect. Well, nearly. We've rearranged the chests.
Every time I close the door of {house}, I think of who built it. Thank you.
I've never lived in a house a friend built. It feels different. Warmer, somehow.
The beds are just right and the door shuts properly. You did a fine job, {player}.
Folk keep asking who built our house. I tell them proudly.
home.newborn_bed: We've a new baby in the family and nowhere for them to sleep. We're making do with a drawer.
The baby needs a bed of their own. Do you know anyone handy with a hammer?
Our little one is sleeping between us for now. Nobody's sleeping much.
A new baby is the best news. A new bed for them would be the second best.
We need a bed for the baby. They're very small, but they take up a surprising amount of room.
If anyone has a spare cot, we have a very small person who would like it.
home.partner_moved: I've moved in with {partner}! Our things are all muddled together now. I love it.
We finally share a house. I keep waking up and forgetting where I am, and then I remember, and I smile.
{partner} and I have a home together now. Two of everything, and one of us always loses the other's socks.
Moving in together was the best decision we've made. Apart from deciding which side of the bed is whose.
Our house, not mine and not theirs. Ours. I like the sound of that.
home.vacant: There's an empty bed down the lane now. Nobody's had the heart to sleep in it.
I walk past that empty house and still expect a light in the window.
Someone will move in eventually, I suppose. It won't be the same.
The bed's still made, just as they left it. Nobody wants to change that yet.
A house goes very quiet when someone's gone. You can feel it from the street.
We keep the step swept at the empty house. It seems like the right thing to do.
home.bedtime: I'm off home. My bed's been calling me since supper.
Time for me to head back to {house}. Goodnight, {player}.
Home, slippers, bed. In that order, and quickly.
I'm going home before my eyes close by themselves.
Can't stop, it's late. The lamp's lit at home and someone's waiting.
Goodnight! If I'm not home soon somebody will start worrying.
home.carried: I woke up in my own bed. Last I knew I was lying in the dirt. Somebody carried me home.
The apothecary patched me up and had me brought home. There's nowhere better to mend.
I came round under my own blanket, with my own ceiling above me. Best sight in the world.
They tell me I was carried home after I went down. My head hurts, but my pillow helps.
Waking up at home after a fright like that... I nearly cried. Maybe I did a little.
home.carried.cot: I woke up on the apothecary's cot. Not my bed, but a kind one.
The apothecary kept me overnight on the cot. Smelled of herbs and worry.
I've been on the cot at the apothecary's. They wouldn't let me leave until I could stand.
I came round at the apothecary's with a blanket over me and a bitter tea beside me.
No bed of my own to go to, so they kept me on the cot. I'm grateful all the same.
baby.home.mine: I've got my own bed! It's got a squeaky bit if you bounce in the middle!
My room is the best room. It has a window AND a spider.
I sleep right next to my mum and dad's room. In case of monsters.
Want to see my bed? I made it myself! Well, I put the pillow on.
Our house is the best house in the whole village. I checked all of them.
I have a secret hiding place in my house. I'm not telling you where. Under the bed.
baby.home.new: We moved to a new house! I've got a new bed and it doesn't creak yet!
Our new house is SO big! Well, bigger. I can do a whole cartwheel in it.
I got a new bed! It's just for me! Nobody else's feet!
We live in a different house now. I keep going to the old one by mistake.
home.plaque.lived: The doorstep is worn smooth by the people who live here.
Boots by the door, smoke from the chimney: somebody calls this home.
A well-loved house. You can tell by the scuffs on the step.
Someone has polished this plaque recently.
The windowsill has a flower on it, and someone remembers to water it.
Somewhere inside, a kettle is probably on.
home.plaque.empty: Nobody lives here yet. The house is waiting.
An empty house, swept and ready for someone.
The beds are made and nobody has slept in them.
Quiet inside. It needs people to make it a home.
home.plaque.private: Private. Nobody will move in uninvited.
A private house: the village knows to leave it be.
This house is kept private. Residents won't settle here.
notice.house: We need a bigger house. If anyone can build one, my family would be ever so grateful. - {name}
Wanted: a house for a family in {village}. A roof, a door, and beds enough for all of us. - {name}
Please, somebody, build us a home. We'll keep it clean, we'll keep it warm, and we'll never forget who built it.
Help wanted: a builder with a kind heart. We need somewhere to live. - {name}
Does anyone have the know-how to build a house? Ours has run out of room, or we've run out of house. - {name}
Notice: house needed. Beds needed. Patience running out. Gratitude guaranteed. - {name}
We're making do, but we can't make do much longer. A house with enough beds would change everything. - {name}
To any builder passing through {village}: a family here needs a home. Put up a House Plaque so we know it's ours.
notice.house.homeless: I haven't got a home in {village}. Could someone build a little house with a bed in it? - {name}
Wanted: four walls, a roof and a bed. For me. I've been sleeping wherever I can. - {name}
I'd be so grateful for a house of my own. Even a small one. Even a very small one. - {name}
Somebody without a bed is looking for one. That somebody is me. Please help. - {name}
A home for someone who hasn't got one. That's all I'm asking. - {name}
notice.house.crowded: We need a bigger house! There are more of us than beds, and someone always ends up on the floor. - {name}
Our family is split between two houses. Could someone build one big enough for all of us? - {name}
Wanted: a house with more beds than we've got now. Elbows in faces nightly. Please help. - {name}
We've outgrown our house. Lovingly, but completely. A bigger one would be a dream. - {name}
Too many of us, too few beds. If you can build, we'd be forever in your debt. - {name}
notice.house.newborn: We have a new baby and nowhere to put them! A house with a bed for the little one, please. - {name}
New baby, same old house, not enough beds. Could someone build us a home with room to grow? - {name}
Wanted: a cot or a house with one. Our newest arrival is sleeping in a drawer. - {name}
The baby needs a bed of their own, and we need a little more room. Can anyone help? - {name}
A new life has come to {village}! Now it needs a place to sleep. Please help us build one. - {name}
notice.thanks.house: You built us a house! I don't know what to say. Thank you, from all of us.
We moved in last night. Everybody slept. Everybody! Thank you, {player}.
A home. You gave us a home. I'll never walk past it without thinking of you.
Thank you for the house! The beds are wonderful. The door shuts. It's perfect.
I've already put a flower on the windowsill. Thank you for building it.
Thank you, {player}. When people ask who built our house, I'll say a friend did.
Our family is under one roof again, thanks to you. Thank you.
Here, take this, and know you're welcome at our table any night.
baby.notice.house: We need a bigger house! My brother kicks in his sleep and I need my own bed!
Can you build us a house? With a tower? It doesn't need a tower. But a tower would be nice.
I sleep on the floor right now! It's a bit fun but mostly it's lumpy.
We need a new house because there's a new baby and the baby is LOUD.
If you build us a house, I'll help! I'm good at carrying very small blocks.
Please make us a house! I'll draw you a picture of it when it's done!
homesteader.greet: Welcome to {place}. Mind the hens, they think they own the path.
Oh! A visitor. We get more foxes than visitors out here.
Hello, {player}. Wipe your boots if you're going anywhere near the kitchen.
Morning, noon or night, you're welcome at {place}.
Ah, a face that isn't covered in feathers. Hello!
Hello there. You've walked a long way to find us, I'd wager.
Good to see you. Pull up a hay bale and sit.
Hello! You've caught me between one chore and the next. That's where I always am.
Welcome. Mind the well, the rope's older than I am.
Well, look at that. Company!
Hello, {player}. The kettle's on. It's always on.
If you've come for the quiet, you've found the right farm.
Hello! Step round the carrots, would you? They're shy.
Ah, {player}. The road's brought you round to us again.
You'll stay a while? It's a long walk back to anywhere.
Hello. If you hear shouting, that's just me arguing with the scarecrow.
Good day! I'd wave, but my hands are full of something. They usually are.
Hello. {place} is a lot of chickens and not many people. Glad you're here to even it up.
Hello! {partner}'s about somewhere. Follow the sound of grumbling.
Welcome to {place}. My {spouse} and I built it, mostly out of stubbornness.
Hello, {player}! {partner} saw you coming from the top field and sent me to say so.
Oh, hello. Don't tell {partner}, but I was having a sit-down.
Welcome! My {spouse} will be glad of a new face. So will I. We've worn ours out on each other.
If {partner} offers you pie, say yes. If {partner} offers you advice, also say yes, then do as you like.
Hello! You've just missed {partner}. Or {partner}'s just missed you. Hard to say which.
Ah, a visitor! My {spouse} will want every word you say repeated at supper, so speak slowly.
Hello. The gate sticks. Lift it and mutter at it, that's how my {spouse} does it.
homesteader.greet.stranger: Oh. A stranger. We don't see many folk out this way. What brings you?
Hello... You're not lost, are you? Nobody comes out here unless they're lost.
Stay where I can see you a moment. Right. You look honest enough. Welcome.
A traveller? You'll have walked far. There's water in the well, help yourself.
I don't know you, but you look like you could use a sit-down.
We don't get callers. You'll forgive me for staring.
Hello, stranger. Close the gate behind you, the hens are plotting something.
You're not a peddler, are you? We've nothing to buy and less to spend.
Who's there? Oh. Just a traveller. My heart was going like a butter churn.
Come in off the road, then. Nobody should be out here alone after dark.
{partner}! Someone at the gate! ...It's all right, they look harmless.
{partner} says I'm too trusting with strangers. Please don't prove {partner} right.
homesteader.greet.friend: {player}! I was hoping you'd come by. I saved you the brown egg.
There's my favourite traveller. Come in, come in.
Back again! You're practically a neighbour now. Our only one.
{partner} bet me a turnip you'd turn up this week. I've lost a turnip, and I don't mind a bit.
Ah, it's you. Even the hens stopped squawking. They know you now.
Good to see you, friend. There's a dent in the bench by the well that's yours by rights.
{player}! Sit, sit. Tell me everything the world's been up to.
My {spouse} lit an extra lantern at the gate last night, in case you came. And here you are.
Hello, dear friend. You've the look of someone who hasn't eaten. We'll fix that.
Ha! I knew that walk. Nobody else crosses a field quite like you do.
Look who it is! {place} feels a lot less far from everywhere when you visit.
You came back. I never quite believe it till I see you at the gate.
homesteader.greet.morning: Morning! The hens beat you to it. They always do.
Good morning. I've been up since before the birds. The birds were rude about it.
Morning, {player}. There's porridge if you're quick and {partner} isn't.
Fresh morning, fresh eggs. Couldn't ask for more.
Morning. The dew's still on the wheat. Best hour of the day, this.
Good morning! It's {time} and I've already fed, watered and argued with everything that lives here.
homesteader.greet.evening: Evening, {player}. The field goes gold about now. Stand here and look.
Good evening. Day's work done, or near enough to lie about it.
Evening! Supper's on. You could smell it from the gate, I expect.
Evening. {partner} and I sit on the step about now and say nothing at all. Come and join us.
Good evening. The swallows are flying low, so the weather will turn.
Evening. I'll be lighting the lanterns soon. Out here, you light them early.
homesteader.greet.night: It's dark, {player}. Come inside the fence, quick.
You're out late. Wolves were howling up on the ridge an hour ago.
Hush, {partner}'s asleep. One creak of that gate and the whole farm's awake.
Goodness, it's {time}! What are you doing out in the dark?
Come in by the lantern. Nothing good walks the fields at this hour.
Oh, {player}. I was just making sure the coop's barred. Twice. Three times.
homesteader.weather.rain: Rain! The wheat's been begging for it. Me, less so.
Listen to that on the roof. Best sound in the world, once the hay's in.
Rain again. {partner} will be in soon, dripping all over my clean floor.
The well will be glad of this. So will the carrots. So will I, once I'm dry.
Rain's good for the field and bad for the knees. Mine know it's coming before the clouds do.
Wet hens are the angriest creatures alive. Mind yourself near the coop today.
homesteader.weather.thunder: Thunder! Get under a roof, {player}. The open field's no place to be in this.
The hens are under the cart and I'd quite like to join them.
My {spouse} counts the seconds between the flash and the rumble. I count the hens.
A storm like this, you pray it doesn't set the haystack alight.
Every crack of that, I think of the old oak by the stream. It's been struck twice already.
homesteader.weather.snow: Snow on the field. Nothing to do but mend things and eat stew.
Snow! It'll be a cold walk to the well tomorrow.
Our first winter here, the snow came up to the windowsills. This is nothing.
I love the snow. Everything goes quiet, even the hens.
Snow brings the wolves down closer. Keep near the house tonight.
homesteader.weather.clearing: There's the sun again. Everything smells of wet earth and good luck.
Rain's done. Out we go. The weeds will have grown an inch while we weren't looking.
Look at the field shine! Worth every drop.
Cleared up nicely. I'll put the washing back out and dare it to rain again.
homesteader.weather.hot: Hot as a bread oven out there. The hens are lying flat as pancakes.
Days like this I haul water till my arms ache. The wheat drinks it faster than I can pour.
Too hot to work, too much work to stop. That's farming in a nutshell.
Find some shade, {player}. The north side of the haystack's cool, if you don't mind the itch.
homesteader.chat: I counted the carrot rows this morning. Still the same number. I check anyway.
Duchess laid in my boot again. She's the boss of that coop and she knows it.
It's a long walk to market. Long enough to forget what you went for, which I always do.
The quiet out here takes some getting used to. Then you can't live without it.
Mended the fence, fed the hens, drew the water. Now I'm talking to you. A good day, all told.
I spent the whole morning chasing Nettle. That hen could escape from a locked chest.
Nobody rings a bell to wake me out here. The sun does it, and it's much politer about it.
There's a fox been sniffing round the coop. I've sat up two nights with a lantern.
Some days the work never ends. Some days it ends and I go looking for more.
Warm bread and a full well. I've stopped asking for more than that.
I talk to the carrots. They grow better for it. Don't tell anyone.
The haystack's leaning again. I've propped it with a plank and a prayer.
The well bucket came up with a frog in it this morning. I put him back. He seemed offended.
It's {weekday}, they tell me. Out here every day's called Workday.
I miss the tavern singing back in {village}. I don't miss the tavern singer.
Saw a deer at the edge of the wheat at dawn. We looked at each other for a long while.
I've been mending the hen house roof. The hens supervised. Badly.
You can see the weather coming for miles out here. Doesn't make it come any slower.
Barnaby the scarecrow lost his hat in the wind. The crows have been laughing at him all day.
There's a crack in the big jug. It's been there twenty years. It'll outlast me.
My hands smell of onions and earth. Honest smells, both.
Nobody out here knows my business. Nobody but the hens, and they only gossip among themselves.
I've been saving seed from the best ears of wheat. Next year's field is in a sack up in the loft.
Pudding laid three eggs this week. She's very proud. We're all very proud.
Washing day. Every sheet's on the line and the sky's thinking about rain. Typical.
I made a new handle for the hoe. It's crooked, but then so am I these days.
A day like this, I wouldn't swap {place} for a castle.
Found an old arrowhead in the furrow. Somebody's adventure ended here, a long time ago.
The wild bees have found the clover by the well. If I can find their nest, there'll be honey.
It's {season}, and the field knows it before I do.
I sang to the hens this morning. Duchess walked out halfway through. Everyone's a critic.
Out here you learn to fix things. Or you learn to live with them broken.
Scraps go to the hens, and the eggs come back. Nothing's wasted on a farm, not even the peelings.
I sat on the step after supper and watched a storm pass three valleys over. Better than any play.
My back aches, my feet ache, and the field looks wonderful. A fair trade.
{partner} and I had a row about where the new fence post goes. It went exactly where I said. Then we moved it.
My {spouse} has been whistling all morning. Either the wheat's looking good or something's been broken and hidden.
{partner} burnt the porridge. I said nothing. I'm saving it for a later argument.
My {spouse} snores like a pig in clover. I'd miss it if it stopped.
{partner} found a four-leafed clover by the well and gave it to me. It's pressed in the almanac now.
I caught {partner} talking to the scarecrow again. Barnaby was winning the argument.
{partner} wants a second hen house. We have one hen house. It's full of opinions already.
Some evenings {partner} reads the almanac aloud, and I'm asleep by the second page. Every time.
My {spouse} swears the moon makes the carrots grow. I swear it's the muck. We're both half right.
{partner} and I don't say much while we work. After all these years, you don't need to.
{partner} has been in a mood since the fox got in. Can't blame anybody but the fox.
My {spouse} has started naming the carrots. I've said it'll only end in tears at supper.
homesteader.chat.new: We don't get many visitors. You'll have to forgive my manners, they've gone rusty.
What brings you all the way out here? Lost, or looking?
This is {place}. It's not much, but we carried every stone of it ourselves.
Just a little farm. Wheat, carrots, hens, and more mud than you'd think possible.
You've come from {village}, maybe? Is the old bell still ringing everyone awake at dawn?
I'm {name}, and my {spouse} is {partner}. That's the whole household, if you don't count the hens. You should count the hens.
Don't mind me asking questions. News doesn't walk out this far on its own.
You're welcome to water from the well. Just don't drop the bucket, it took a whole day to fish out last time.
We came out here for the quiet. You're the least noisy thing that's happened all week.
Are you a trader? A wanderer? We get one of each a year, if that.
homesteader.chat.close: Some nights I lie awake and wonder what happens to this farm when we're too old to work it.
We never had children. Some years that sits lighter than others. This is a light year, with you about.
I left {village} because I was tired of being who everyone there thought I was. Out here I'm just me.
The truth? The dark frightens me. The dark beyond the fence, every night. You don't stop being scared. You just bar the door.
Sometimes I think we were fools to leave. Then the sun comes up over the wheat and I know we weren't.
You're the nearest thing to family we've got out here, {player}. I hope you know that.
I'm getting slower. The field's the same size it always was, but somehow it's grown.
When I was young I wanted adventures. Now I want the hens to lay and the roof to hold. Funny how that goes.
If anything ever happens to us, would you look in on the hens? Daft thing to ask. I'm asking anyway.
My hands shake a little in the mornings now. I hide it. I'm telling you because you won't fuss.
I keep a little box of letters from home. Nobody writes any more, so I read the old ones.
I hope I go first. Selfish, I know. I couldn't bear {place} without {partner} in it.
{partner} still holds my hand on the walk back from the well. Every single time. Don't tell anyone.
We wanted little ones, {partner} and I. It never happened. We poured it all into this place instead.
Some winter nights I watch {partner} asleep by the fire and think: we did it. We actually did it.
Leaving {village} was {partner}'s idea. I was frightened. I'd have followed {partner} off a cliff, though, and this was only a hill.
I worry about my {spouse}'s cough. Every winter it comes back a little worse.
When we're old and grey, {partner} and I will sit on that step and argue about which of us is greyer.
homesteader.past: Our first winter here, the well froze solid. We melted snow in the stewpot for six weeks.
The hard winter, we burned the spare chair. Then the other spare chair. We hadn't many chairs to begin with.
I grew up in {village}. The bell every morning, the bell every evening, and gossip in between.
The council in {village} spent a whole season arguing about one fence. That's when I knew I had to go.
When we first came out here, there was nothing but grass and a stream. We slept under the cart for a month.
The first carrot we ever pulled from this field was the size of my little finger. We cut it in half and ate it like a feast.
The first year, wolves took two of our hens. I learned to sleep with one ear open.
I carried the stones for the farmhouse up from the riverbed, two at a time. My shoulders still remember.
Old Mistress Hobb back in {village} knew what you'd had for supper before you'd finished eating it. I do not miss Mistress Hobb.
The baker in {village} used to slip me a sweet roll every market day. I still miss that roll.
That first harvest, we had so little wheat we could count the sheaves on our fingers. We cried anyway. The good sort of crying.
The hard winter was the year we learned what we were made of. Turnips, mostly. Turnips were all we had.
Folk in {village} said we'd be back within the year. That was a long time ago now.
The hard winter, wolves circled the house three nights running. Nobody slept. The hens didn't even lay.
{partner} and I met at a harvest dance. One of us stepped on the other's feet all night. We still argue about which.
We were married in {village} in the spring, and the very next week {partner} and I pushed one cart out here with everything we owned on it.
My {spouse} built the hen house that first summer. It leaned. It still leans. The hens don't seem to mind.
The hard winter, {partner} walked to {village} through snow up to the knees for a sack of flour. I've never been so frightened, nor so glad to see anyone come home.
homesteader.night: Listen. That's an owl. That's the wind. And that... that's a zombie. Inside, now.
I check the coop door every night before bed. Then I check it again. Then {partner} checks it.
Nights out here are darker than any you'll have seen in {village}. No lanterns but ours for miles.
Every night I bar the door and think: one more day done. One more day kept.
Something hissed out by the haystack. I've decided it was a cat. I've decided very firmly.
The stars are so thick out here you could spread them on bread.
My {spouse} sleeps with the pitchfork by the bed. I've stopped asking why.
At night the wheat whispers. It's the wind, probably. Probably.
homesteader.work: A farm's like a clock with a hundred hands. Something always needs winding.
Wheat, carrots, eggs, bread. Everything we eat, we grew it or coaxed it out of a hen.
We split the work down the middle. The middle moves about, depending on who's tired.
The fence takes more mending than anything. Wolves test it, the wind tests it, and Nettle tests it daily.
Everything here does two jobs. The haystack's a windbreak, the well keeps the butter cool, and the cart's a table on market day.
We take the cart to market twice a season. Wheat and eggs go out. Salt, nails and news come back.
You don't own a farm. It owns you. It just lets you sleep in it.
If the well, the field and the hens are all happy, it's a good day. Two out of three, I'll take.
{partner} and I meet by the well at noon. Bread, cheese, and a report on everything that's gone wrong.
My {spouse} and I have a rule: no quarrels till the work's done. So we quarrel at supper.
homesteader.work.farmer: Ploughed the top field today. The ground's heavy this year. The plough came up with half the hill on it.
Barnaby the scarecrow has my old hat now. He wears it better than I ever did.
The wheat's coming in tall. Another fortnight and it'll be up to my belt.
Sowing's a matter of faith. You put good seed into the dark and trust it.
Crows took a whole row of seed. I've moved Barnaby closer. He looks a little more fearsome now. A little.
Carrots want loose soil and patience. I can manage one of those.
Harvest's the best week of the year and the worst week for my back.
I walk the field end to end every evening. Looking for blight, mostly. Mostly just looking.
My {spouse} says I'd sleep in the field if I could. I have. Twice. Both harvest moons.
I saved the best seed from last year in a clay pot. It's the most precious thing we own.
The soil here was all roots and stones when we came. Took three years to turn it sweet.
Hoe in the morning, water at noon, weed at dusk. A field's never finished. Only resting.
A good rain at the right time is worth more than a sack of emeralds to a farmer.
{partner} brings me bread out in the field at noon. It's the bit of the day I look forward to most.
I've moved the carrots to the lower field this year. Wheat wears the ground out if you let it.
homesteader.work.cook: The oven's been going since dawn. Three loaves, a pie, and something I'm calling an experiment.
Duchess has stopped laying in the coop and started laying in my bread basket. We're negotiating.
I've put up forty jars of carrot preserve. Forty. We'll be orange by spring.
Bread needs warmth, time and a firm hand. Same as most things worth having.
The hearth fire hasn't gone out in a year. I bank it every night like I'm tucking in a sleeping child.
I make bread from wheat {partner} grew, in an oven we built, on a farm that's ours. Every loaf tastes of that.
Pudding's been laying like she's being paid for it. There are eggs in every bowl in the house.
Keeping house out here means sweeping half the field out of the door every evening. It walks in on boots.
Stew today. It's always stew on washing day, and nobody's allowed to argue on washing day.
I'm salting down the last of the carrots for winter. A full larder's the best lock on any door.
My {spouse} tracks mud straight across a floor I've just scrubbed, then compliments me on the floor.
I keep the honey cakes in a tin with a stiff lid. It stops the mice, and it slows down {partner}.
The hens know the sound of the scrap bucket from the far end of the field. They come running like it's market day.
I found wild thyme growing by the stream. The soup's never been happier.
Churned butter all morning. My arms are tired, but the bread won't be lonely tonight.
homesteader.adventure: If you're crossing the hills, stop by a stream before dark. Water and a fire, and you'll live to tell it.
Adventures? Mine is getting the cart to market without losing a wheel. Yours sound grander.
Take some eggs for the road. Hard-boiled. They travel better than you'd think.
When I was young I wanted to see the sea. I still might. Once the harvest's in. It's always once the harvest's in.
Mind the pillagers on the high road. They've banners and crossbows and no manners at all.
Wherever you end up, there's a bed at {place} if you need one.
Bring me back a seed from somewhere strange. I'll find a corner of the field for it.
I followed a stream once, just to see where it went. It went to a bog. Very educational.
Don't go into the caves without a lantern and a way back. The dark down there doesn't give things back easily.
{partner} says an adventure is just a bad day you tell well afterwards. Coming out to {place} was one of those.
My {spouse} and I had our adventure. We walked out of {village} with a cart and never walked back.
If you pass a peddler in a green hat, tell them {partner} is still waiting on the needles we paid for.
homesteader.joke: Why did the scarecrow get a medal? He was outstanding in his field. Barnaby's still waiting on his.
I tried telling the carrots a joke this morning. Nothing. Tough crowd, root vegetables.
Duchess crossed the road once. Never mind why. She came back and told the other hens it wasn't worth it.
What did the wheat say to the farmer? "Stop staring. I'm growing as fast as I can."
Why do hens make poor secret-keepers? They can't hold anything in. They just lay it all out.
What's the hardest thing about farming? The ground. Ha! I've been waiting all week to say that.
Our well is so deep the bucket comes up with yesterday's water in it.
The fox asked if he could join the hens for supper. "As a guest," he said. The hens still said no. Clever hens.
How many farmers does it take to mend a fence? Two. One to mend it, and one to say it was fine the way it was.
{partner} lost a needle in the haystack once. Looked all afternoon. Found three other needles, a spoon and Nettle.
My {spouse} says I'm the finest singer in the valley. I'm also the only singer in the valley.
homesteader.news: News? Out here? A hen laid a double yolk. That's been the biggest thing all month.
The last peddler through here said {village} has a new baker. I'm too far off to try the bread, so it hardly matters.
I heard at market that pillagers were seen on the north road. Mind how you go.
No news is good news, my mother used to say. We get a great deal of good news out here.
You tell me the news, {player}. You're the one who's been somewhere.
Market day's coming. I'll hear a month's gossip in one afternoon and spend a week sorting out what's true.
A wandering tinker said there'd been a wedding in {village}. Couldn't remember whose. Told us all about the cake, though.
The fox is back. That's the news. That's all the news there is.
My {spouse} came home from market with three stories, two rumours and no salt. We had to go back for the salt.
{partner} swears the peddler said the council in {village} has banned whistling on {weekday}s. I'll believe it when I hear the silence.
homesteader.heart: Anyone special? There's only ever been one. Still is.
Ha! You've met the other half of this farm. That's my answer.
Special? I married the most stubborn soul in the valley. I'd do it again tomorrow.
Love isn't flowers out here. It's someone carrying the water when your back's bad.
You'll find my answer in the field or in the kitchen, depending on the hour.
Who do you think? The one who's been shouting my name across the yard all morning.
{partner}. It's always been {partner}. Who else would put up with me?
My {spouse}, of course. Even when we're quarrelling. Especially then, oddly.
I still go pink when {partner} looks at me a certain way. At my age! Don't laugh.
I knew {partner} was the one when we split our last heel of bread and neither of us would take the bigger half.
My {spouse} is the reason I get up before the sun. Well. That and the hens.
homesteader.player.hurt: You're bleeding! Sit down on the step. I've clean cloth and a strong opinion about this.
What happened to you? Wolves? Come here, let me see.
You look like you lost a fight with a hedge. Or with something worse than a hedge.
There's honey and yarrow in the kitchen. Good for cuts. Come on, in you go.
Hold still. I've patched up {partner} more times than I can count. You're in safe hands.
homesteader.player.hungry: You look half-starved. There's bread in the oven and nobody's allowed to argue with me about it.
Hungry? On a farm? Not while I'm standing. Sit.
Your stomach's louder than our hens. Let's put something in it.
You've got that hollow look. There's stew on the hearth and an egg with your name on it.
homesteader.player.dark: It's black as a cellar out there. Stay by the lanterns.
Out here the dark's thicker than in any village. Keep near the house.
Don't wander off the path at night. The field looks different in the dark, and so does whatever's in it.
homesteader.player.wet: You're dripping like a washing line! Stand by the hearth.
Soaked through! Give me that cloak, I'll hang it by the fire.
Wet as a hen in a ditch. Come in before you catch your death.
homesteader.held.sword: Put that {item} away, you'll frighten the hens off laying.
That {item} looks sharp. Use it on the wolves, mind, not on my fence.
Out here, a friend with that {item} is a welcome sight after dark.
I've never held anything sharper than a scythe. That {item} looks a good deal less friendly.
homesteader.held.flower: Oh, that {item} is lovely. I'll put it in a cup on the windowsill, if you're giving it away.
Where did you find that {item}? The meadow past the stream? I always mean to go and look.
That {item} would brighten the kitchen. Nothing grows that pretty out here except the weeds.
My {spouse} picked me flowers the day we arrived here. That {item} puts me in mind of them.
homesteader.held.food: That {item} smells good. Not as good as fresh bread, but nothing does.
Eating on the walk? Sit down and eat that {item} properly, you'll give yourself hiccups.
Is that {item} from market? We grow our own, but I'll not turn up my nose at a bite.
That {item}'s all very well, but wait till you taste what comes out of our oven.
homesteader.held.emerald: Put that {item} away. There's nothing out here to spend it on but eggs, and eggs are free to friends.
That {item} would buy a lot of nails at market. We always need nails.
Careful flashing that {item} about out here. Pillagers can smell it, I swear.
We once traded a whole cart of wheat for less than that {item}. Shiny, isn't it?
herbalist.greet: Ah. {player}. The kettle's on and the nettles are drying. Mind your head on the rafters.
Welcome to {place}. Don't touch anything purple.
You walk like someone with a question. Most people who come up this path do.
Back again? Either you like my company or something's ailing you. I'll guess which.
The bees told me someone was coming. They're terrible gossips.
Wipe your boots. Moss is lovely on a roof and dreadful on a floor.
Hello, {player}. You smell of the road. Sit; I'll find you something that smells better.
You came in daylight. That alone makes you rarer than most of my visitors.
Come in, come in. Duck under the elderflower; it's drying, and it bruises if you look at it wrong.
Good. A visitor who knocks. You'd be surprised how many just stand at the gate and whisper.
{player}. I wondered when the forest would send you back.
The cauldron's simmering, so keep your voice down. It sulks if you shout.
Hello. Whatever it is, I've heard worse, and I've cured most of it.
Mind the third step. It's been crooked longer than I have.
You've burrs on your hem and a question on your face. Out with the question; the burrs can wait.
Come to see the witch at the edge of the woods? Only teasing. Mostly.
Ah, it's you. The hive went quiet when you came up the path. From bees, that's a compliment.
Another visitor! At this rate I'll have to own a second chair.
Come in. Leave your troubles by the door with the muddy boots. Collect them on the way out, if you still want them.
Hello, {player}. The garden says it's {season}. My knees say it's always winter.
You found {place} again. Most people only manage to find it in the dark.
Hm. You look well. That's either good luck or good sense, and I only keep a remedy for the lack of one.
Welcome back. Sit anywhere that isn't drying, steeping or asleep.
{weekday} already? The week runs faster up here, with no bells to count it by.
herbalist.greet.stranger: A stranger at my gate. Lost, curious or sent? Don't answer. Your boots already told me.
I don't know you. The bees don't know you. Stand still a moment and let us all have a look.
You're not from {village}. Their folk come at night and won't meet my eye. You're looking straight at me.
Hm. A new face. Most people find {place} when they need something. What is it you need?
Stay on the path, stranger. The garden bites, and not all of it is nettles.
Name's {name}. You'll have heard other names for me, I expect. They're less accurate.
Strangers who come by day want directions. Strangers who come by night want something else. Which are you?
You've wandered a long way from anywhere. So did I, on purpose. Did you?
Don't fret, stranger. Whatever they told you down the hill, I've never turned anyone into anything.
herbalist.greet.friend: {player}! Come in. I saved you the good honey. The bees argued; I won.
There you are. I set out two cups this morning without thinking. Now I know why.
My favourite visitor. Don't tell the moths; they think it's them.
Ah, {player}. Sit by the fire. You're the only one who calls in daylight and isn't ashamed of it.
Good to see you, friend. The garden's been asking after you. Well. The weeds have.
You came back. People don't, usually, once they're cured. I'm glad you're not the usual sort.
Hello, you. I've a jar with your name on it. Truly; I wrote it on the lid.
Friend! Mind the rafters, mind the cauldron, mind nothing else. Make yourself at home.
{player}, you're a sight. A good one. Better than foxglove in bloom, and a great deal safer.
herbalist.greet.morning: Morning. The dew's still on the yarrow, so I'm picking. Talk while I work.
Early, aren't you? Good. Herbs picked before the sun is high keep their tempers.
Morning, {player}. The bees were up before both of us, and they want you to know it.
Dawn's the honest hour. Nobody comes asking for anything they're ashamed of before breakfast.
Good morning. I've been up since the owls went to bed. Tea?
herbalist.greet.evening: Evening. The lanterns will be lit down in {village} soon, and then this path gets busy.
Good evening. Sit a while. Soon I'll be answering the door to people who'll swear tomorrow they never came.
Evening, {player}. Dusk is when the moths visit the garden. They're the only callers I never charge.
Evening. The light's gone golden. That's the herbs' favourite hour, and mine.
herbalist.greet.night: Oh, it's you. I thought you were another one from {village}, come for something they'll pretend they never needed.
Knocking at {time}? You'd fit right in with my usual callers. What ails you?
Night callers get the back door and no questions. You can have the front door, {player}. You're not ashamed of me.
Come in quickly. There are things on the path at this hour, and only some of them are customers.
Shh. I've a pot on for someone's broken heart. They'll be back for it any moment, and they won't want an audience.
It's late, so I'll assume you need something. Everyone who comes after dark does.
herbalist.weather.rain: Rain! The moss on my roof is having the time of its life.
Let it pour. The garden's been sulking for a week; this will cheer it right up.
Wet weather brings out the mushrooms and the slugs. One of those I'm pleased to see.
Rain on the roof and something on the boil. There are worse ways to spend a day.
Come under the eaves. Nettles gathered in the rain sting less, but you're not a nettle.
herbalist.weather.thunder: Folk say lightning once struck a farmer out by the swamp and they woke up a witch. Folk say a lot of things about me, too.
Thunder sours milk and sweetens elderflower. Or so Sorrel swore. I've never managed to prove either.
Stay in till it passes. The cauldron hates thunder; it rattles its lid like it wants to answer back.
Storms bring the night callers early. Fear makes people remember their coughs.
herbalist.weather.snow: Snow. The garden's asleep, and so should I be. Instead I'm grinding dried yarrow by the fire.
Everything's under white. Good. The bees are snug, and the gossip from the village can't climb the hill.
Snow's a blanket for the roots. Under it, everything's quietly planning for spring.
herbalist.weather.clearing: There, it's lifting. Go and smell the garden now; it won't smell this good again till the next rain.
Sky's clearing. The bees will be out in a moment, cross about the delay.
The clouds are breaking. Wet petals bruise, so I'll wait an hour before I pick. You can wait with me.
herbalist.weather.hot: Hot enough to dry herbs on the doorstep. Saves me climbing to the rafters.
Too warm for the cauldron. Too warm for anything but sitting in the shade and judging the bees.
Drink something. In this heat a body wilts faster than lettuce, and it's harder to revive.
herbalist.chat: Folk in {village} call me a witch behind my back. To my face they call me "please" and "it's only a little cough".
Never eat a mushroom somebody else picked unless you'd trust them with your life. That's not a saying. That's a rule.
A bee never visits the same flower twice in a morning. Don't go back for more from what's already given you everything.
Pick leaves by the waxing moon and roots by the waning. Does it matter? It matters to me, and I'm the one picking.
Old saying: "Where nettles grow, good soil lies below." Same's true of some people.
Foxglove is beautiful and it will stop your heart. I grow it at the back of the garden so I always know exactly where it is.
Dandelions are a weed to everyone but me. Leaves for salad, root for the liver, seeds for wishing. Nothing wasted.
The trouble with being needed is that people resent you for it.
Yarrow stops bleeding. Honey keeps a wound clean. A kind word does neither, but it doesn't hurt to have one handy.
My roof's more moss than slate. I keep it that way. It holds the warmth, and the wrens love it.
Lily of the valley smells like heaven and is poison from root to bell. Never eat it. Never let a child near it.
A saying of mine: "Sweet berries, sour thorns, and the bush apologises for neither."
The village buys honey from me at market and swears it came from someone else's hive. My bees know their own work.
Glow berries are the only lamp that needs no oil. I've strung them in the cellar. It's like living under a small, soft sky.
Every remedy is half plant and half listening. Most people can't get the listening anywhere else.
Poppies for sleep, but only a little. Too much and you'll sleep through things you'd rather have been awake for.
Elderflower in spring, elderberries in autumn. The same tree gives you a cordial and a cough syrup. Generous thing.
Want to know whether a stranger's honest? Offer them nettle tea. Liars always say they love it.
I talk to the plants. Not because they listen. Because nobody else up here does.
Cornflowers for tired eyes. I steep them for the scribes in {village}. They squint at me less, after.
Oxeye daisies grow where nobody wants them, and they bloom anyway. I've taken a lesson from that.
The bees and I have an arrangement. I don't take more than I need, and they don't sting more than I deserve.
"Moss grows on the north side," they say. Moss grows wherever it likes. Navigate by the stars, or by sense.
Alliums keep the pests off the roses. Some people are like alliums. They smell a bit odd and the garden's better for them.
Azure bluets are small and plain, and they ease a headache better than anything showy. Remember that.
Brown mushrooms like the dark, the damp, and being left alone. I've always felt we understood each other.
Someone left a basket of eggs at my gate last week. No note. That's how the village says thank you.
A garden is just a long argument with the weather that you occasionally win.
Don't mistake cryptic for wise. I'm cryptic because it makes people leave sooner.
The moon pulls at the water, and every leaf is mostly water. So yes, the moon has opinions about my garden.
Honey never spoils. I've a jar older than some of my visitors. Still sweet.
Sorrel used to say, "Heal the body, then mind your tongue about the rest." I'm still learning the second half.
I hang a sprig of yarrow over the door. Not for luck. It's just where I keep the yarrow.
You'd be amazed what a cup of something warm and a closed door can cure.
"A weed is only a flower nobody has bothered to learn." My own saying. You may borrow it.
If the bees are cross, rain's coming. If I'm cross, someone from the village has been gossiping again.
Zombies leave my garden alone. I'd like to say it's the herbs. It's probably the compost heap.
Moss on the roof, mushrooms in the cellar, bees in the hive. I'm never as alone as people think.
Real witches live in swamp huts and throw bottles and cackle. I've never cackled in my life. Well. Once. It was a good joke.
I could live in {village} if I wanted to. I don't want to. The quiet up here is a remedy too.
herbalist.chat.new: New to these woods? Here's your first piece of advice, free: not every red berry is a sweet berry.
First time at {place}? It's crooked by accident and kept crooked on purpose. Straight houses blow down.
You'll hear stories about me. Half of them are true. I'll not tell you which half.
I'm {name}. I mend what ails people and I keep a garden. The rest of what they say is decoration.
Newcomers always ask two things: "Are you a witch?" and "What's that smell?" No, and elderflower.
If you're staying in these parts, learn where my gate is. You'll need it someday. Everyone does.
Welcome. The rules are simple: knock, don't pick anything, and don't tell the village I was nice to you.
herbalist.chat.close: The one who taught me was called Sorrel. Lived in this very cottage. Knew every plant by name and every person by their cough.
Sorrel used to say the cottage chose who lived in it. When Sorrel died, I came up the path with my bag and the door wasn't locked. I took that as an answer.
I nursed a whole street through a fever one winter. One old man didn't pull through, and he's the only one they remember.
Why do I live apart? A village needs someone to blame and someone to thank. It's easier for them if I'm far enough away to be both.
It costs something, living like this. Nobody brings soup when I'm poorly. I bring it to myself, and I'm a terrible patient.
Some nights I sit on the step and watch the lanterns in {village}, and I think about walking down. Then I think about the faces, and I put the kettle on instead.
Sorrel's hands smelled of yarrow till the very end. Mine are starting to. I didn't expect to be glad of it.
I keep a book of everyone who's come to my door. Not names; just what they needed. It's a thick book, {player}. It's a lonely book.
You're the first person in years who's come up the path without needing anything. Do you know what a gift that is?
I could have been a healer in a big town, with a sign over the door and people who said good morning. I chose the bees. Most days I'd choose them again.
Sorrel's buried under the elder tree. I talk to that tree more than I talk to people. Don't look at me like that; you would too.
The worst part isn't being called a witch. It's someone I sat up all night with crossing the street at market so as not to be seen near me.
If anything happens to me, the recipes are in the tin behind the third jar. You'd know who to give them to. I trust that you would.
herbalist.past: I learned my letters from seed packets and my sums from counting bees. Not the usual schooling.
My first remedy was for my own nettle stings. I was seven and furious, and I've been mixing things ever since.
When I was young I wanted to be a sailor. Then I got seasick on a duck pond. Plants don't rock.
I came to this cottage as an apprentice with one bag and a great many opinions. The opinions got sorted out first.
Sorrel made me weed the garden for a whole year before I was allowed near a pot. I was so cross. I understand now.
The first night someone knocked for a remedy, I was so nervous I gave them the wrong jar. It worked anyway. Faith's strong medicine.
I once spent a whole summer learning the mushrooms of this wood. Don't ask me about them; we'd be here till winter.
There was a time I lived in {village}. Long ago. I had a window box and three friends. I still have the window box.
My mother said I'd grow up strange. She was right, but she said it fondly, and I've held on to that.
Years back a wolf limped into the garden and lay down by the hive and wouldn't leave. I splinted its leg. It visited every winter after, until one winter it didn't.
The first hive I kept swarmed within a week and left me for a hollow oak. Bees, like people, won't be kept against their will.
Before the beehive, before the cauldron, I had a mortar and a mean streak. The mortar's still here. The mean streak's mellowed.
I once walked three days to a market town for a single pot of seeds. Half of them came up foxglove. I've never been so annoyed or so careful.
herbalist.night: Night's when the garden really breathes. Smell that? That's the elder, showing off where nobody can see.
Moths on the window, an owl in the wood, a knock at the door any minute now. That's my night.
It's a {moon} tonight. Sorrel had a rule for every phase. For this one, I think it was "dig the roots and hold your tongue."
Something's shuffling past the garden fence. Zombies, likely. They never come in. I've never asked why.
At night the village forgets it's afraid of me. Funny how that works.
I hear skeletons rattling in the trees some nights. I tell them to keep it down. They never listen.
The bees are asleep. The village is asleep. Just me and the cauldron awake, and it's not much of a talker.
herbalist.work: I'm turning the herbs in the rafters. Leave them hanging one way too long and they dry sulky.
Today's work: nettles for the soup, yarrow for the cuts, poppies for someone who can't sleep and won't say why.
Someone came at midnight for a cough syrup and someone at one for a cure for heartbreak. I gave them both honey. Only one of them knew.
There's a cough working its way through {village}, so the cauldron's full. Elderflower, honey and patience.
Picking dandelions before the rabbits get them. It's a race I lose more often than I'd like.
The brewing stand's bubbling. Don't ask what's in it. You'd only want some.
I'm grinding cornflower petals. Fiddly work. It calms the hands and empties the head.
Three remedies for bad dreams this week. Something's troubling {village}, and it isn't the wolves.
Jars to wash, labels to write, and mushrooms to sort into "stew" and "absolutely not". A busy day.
Smoking the hive to take the honey. The bees know it's coming. We've reached an understanding about how much.
A farmer came this morning for a salve for blistered hands, then asked if I made one for a blistered heart. That one takes longer.
Tying yarrow to dry. Nine stems to a bunch. Sorrel always did nine. I don't know why, and I don't dare change it.
Packing a basket for the old folk down in the valley. They can't climb the hill any more, so the hill goes down to them.
Moss to pack the wound, honey to keep the moss clean. An old trick. Works better than it ought to.
Weeding. The garden grows faster than I can pull, and it's been winning since spring.
Someone wanted a love potion. I gave them a cup of tea and told them to try talking first. That one's free.
herbalist.adventure: Off into the wilds? Take yarrow for cuts and sweet berries for the walk. And come back.
If you find glow berries in a cave, bring me some. I'll trade you a remedy you'll be glad of one day.
There's a swamp a few valleys west with a real witch's hut in it. Don't knock. Unlike me, that one bites.
Out there, every plant is food, medicine or a mistake. Learn which before you're hungry.
Adventure's just a long walk with more bandages. I'll pack you some.
I went after a rare mushroom in a deep cave once. Found it. Also found a creeper. Kept the mushroom, lost an eyebrow.
Bring back stories. And seeds. Mostly seeds.
I don't wander far any more. Everything I need either grows here or comes knocking.
Lost in the woods? Follow the bees. Bees lead to flowers, and tended flowers mean someone's home.
herbalist.joke: Why was the mushroom asked to every feast? Because it was a fun guy. Sorrel told me that one. I've hated it for thirty years and I tell it anyway.
What do you call a bee that can't make up its mind? A maybee. Don't groan; it curdles the honey.
I told the beehive a secret once. By evening the whole garden knew. Never trust anything that buzzes.
Nettle tea: tastes like a meadow, stings like a grudge, and does you more good than either.
Two witches walk into a tavern. I wouldn't know the rest; I've never been invited.
The village says my cottage leans because I cursed it. It leans because the builder liked cider.
People ask why I talk to my plants. Because when I talk to people, they repeat it at market.
Someone asked for a cure for their spouse's snoring. I gave them wool for their ears and the spouse a bowl of nettle soup. Both slept like stones.
herbalist.news: Somebody in {village} is in love and doesn't know how to say it. I won't say who. Their cough was entirely made up.
Three people this week came up for something to help them sleep. Something's keeping the village up at night, and it isn't the bells.
A secret came up the path last night with a bad tooth. I fixed the tooth. The secret stays here.
Someone's planning a proposal on market day. I know because they asked me for something to stop their hands shaking.
There's a quarrel in the village over a fence. Both sides came to me for a headache remedy. Neither knows about the other.
A traveller passing through said pillagers were camped two valleys over. Keep your eyes open on the roads.
Someone's been sneaking honey from my hive at night. It's either a fox or a child. Given the footprints, I'm hoping fox.
I won't name names. But if a certain someone at market tomorrow smells of elderflower, you'll know who couldn't sleep.
herbalist.heart: Remedies for broken hearts are the ones I make most and believe in least. Time's the only real ingredient. The honey's just so it goes down easier.
You're good company, {player}. I don't say that. Ask the bees; they'll tell you I never say that.
I've spent my life listening to everyone else's troubles. It's strange, and lovely, to have someone ask about mine.
When I'm gone, plant something where I used to sit. Not foxglove. Something kind.
Everyone who's knocked on that door at midnight has been at their very worst. I've loved them anyway. That's the work, I think.
Being alone and being lonely are different ailments. I've had both. You've helped with the second.
I've started setting out the second cup before you arrive. Don't let it go to your head.
herbalist.player.hurt: You're bleeding on my floor. Sit. Yarrow first, then the lecture.
Look at the state of you. Hold still. This will sting, and no, I'm not sorry.
Honey on that cut, a clean cloth over it, and stop picking at it. Only children pick, and you're not a child.
What did that to you? Wolves? Skeletons? Your own clumsiness? I'll treat all three, but the last one I'll charge for.
You look like a hedge fought you and won. Come by the fire and let me see.
herbalist.player.hungry: Your stomach's louder than my cauldron. There's nettle soup on the hob. Don't make that face; it's good for you.
You've gone pale round the edges. Eat something, even if it's only sweet berries from the bush by the gate.
A hungry body heals slow and thinks slower. Take some bread and honey before you go anywhere.
herbalist.player.dark: You're blundering about in the dark like a moth that's lost its lamp. Take a sprig of glow berries.
It's black as a cellar out here. Light something, before something else finds you first.
Don't wander about without a light. The things that like the dark don't like visitors.
herbalist.player.wet: You're soaked through. Stand by the fire before you catch something I'll have to cure.
Dripping on my floor like a wet hound. Here, a blanket. And elderflower tea for the chill.
Wet clothes and a cold wind are how most of my winter callers start. Dry off, quickly.
herbalist.held.sword: Put that {item} away in my garden. The bees think it's rude.
That {item} has its uses. Pruning isn't one of them, so keep it off my roses.
You carry that {item} like someone who's needed it. I've cleaned enough wounds to know the look.
herbalist.held.flower: Oh, that {item}. Did you pick it, or did it pick you? Either way, it suits you.
That {item} would dry beautifully, hung upside down by the stem. Or you could just enjoy it. I forget that's allowed.
Keep that {item} in water and out of the sun. Flowers bruise like people do.
You've brought that {item} to a herbalist's door. Like bringing a song to a bard. I'm touched anyway.
Is that {item} for me? No? Then I'll admire it from here.
herbalist.held.food: Eat that {item} slowly. Gulped food sits in the belly like a stone, and I've no remedy for haste.
That {item} is fine, but you'd do better with greens. When did you last eat a nettle? Don't answer.
Don't offer the bees any of that {item}; they'd only complain. Eat it yourself. You look like you need it.
herbalist.held.emerald: Put that {item} away. I don't take money for remedies. I take gossip, eggs and good manners.
That {item} is pretty, but it won't cure a cough. Keep it for market; they'll pretend not to know me there, too.
Folk slip me the odd {item} after dark, then spend the rest in daylight on tonics that don't work.
herbalist.held.potion: Let me see that {item}. Hm. Who brewed this? The colour's off. Shake it before you drink it. Better yet, don't.
That {item} came out of somebody's cauldron, and not mine. Mine would be clearer.
Every bottle like that {item} is a little piece of somebody's garden. Drink it with respect.
pariah.greet: Oh. It's you. I'd ask what you want, but I suspect you'll tell me anyway.
You're standing on my porch. Most people have the decency to stand on the road and stare.
Well? Speak, or move along. The day isn't getting any longer.
Welcome to {place}. Mind the step, it's rotten. Like most things that were once good.
If {village} sent you, you can carry my answer back: no.
I don't get callers. I've arranged my whole life around not getting callers.
Ah, a visitor. How novel. Shall I ring a bell? I used to have one, you know.
Mind the gate. It sticks, and so do I.
You've come a long way to be disappointed. Come in, then.
Hello, {player}. Don't make that face. I said hello, didn't I?
Another day, another wanderer who took the wrong path and found me at the end of it.
I was enjoying the quiet. I'll enjoy it again when you leave.
If you're selling something, I've nothing to buy with. If you're preaching, I've heard it.
What is it? Lost? Curious? Sent? Those are the only three reasons anyone comes up this road.
Good day, you say. I'll be the judge of that. I used to be the judge of a great many things.
You knocked. Nobody knocks anymore. I'd almost forgotten the sound.
Come to see the hermit of {place}? Look your fill. No charge. It's the only thing I give away.
Don't hover in the doorway like a debt collector. In or out.
Hello. There. That was the last courtesy I had left in the cupboard.
I see you found {place}. Congratulations. Most people make a point of not finding it.
Speak up. The wind out here takes words, and I've no patience left to chase them.
Whatever they told you about me in {village}, it was worse than the truth. Or better. I forget which.
Oh, good. Company. Just what the cracked window and I were missing.
Wipe your boots. I may be disgraced, but my floor isn't.
You've got a village look about you. All hope and gossip. Wipe it off before you come any closer.
Hmph. You again, or someone very like you. You all blur together after a while.
Ah. A face. I'd forgotten how much they move about.
pariah.greet.stranger: Who sent you? Don't lie. I sat on a council for eleven years. I know what a lie looks like coming up a path.
I don't know you. Let's keep it that way a little longer.
Stop there. That's close enough for a stranger.
If you've come to gawk at the one they threw out, gawk quickly. I've wood to chop.
Are you from {village}? You've the same way of not quite meeting my eye.
Strangers on my path are either lost or up to something. Which are you?
I'll have your name before you have anything of mine. Not that I've much left.
Nobody walks this far by accident. So what's the errand?
You're new. You'll learn. Everyone does, eventually, and then they stop coming.
Don't smile at me like that. I've been smiled at by better liars than you.
I keep a list of who comes up this road. You're on it now. Congratulations.
Go on, ask. Everyone wants to ask what I did. I'm not telling you.
Keep your hands where I can see them and your pity where I can't.
pariah.greet.friend: Oh, it's you, {player}. Fine. Sit. Not in that chair.
Back again? People will start to talk. Well, they already do. Let them.
I saw you coming from the ridge. I didn't hide. Make of that what you like.
{player}. I suppose I'm not entirely sorry to see you.
You again. The kettle happens to be on. That's a coincidence, nothing more.
I left the gate unlatched. The wind must have done it. Come in.
Ah, my one regular caller. You'll ruin my reputation. Such as it is.
Hmph. You're late. Not that I was expecting you. Not that I keep a clock for it.
There you are. I'd started to think you'd come to your senses.
You look half frozen. Sit by the fire and stop dripping on my good floor.
{player}. Good. I've been saving up a complaint, and there's nobody else to give it to.
Well, if it isn't the only person in the world with worse judgement than {village}.
I swept the step this morning. For no one in particular. Come up, then.
pariah.greet.morning: Morning. The bells in {village} will be ringing about now. I can just hear them, if I'm feeling cruel to myself.
You're up early. So am I. Bitterness makes a fine alarm.
Morning. The dew's on the fence, the porridge is burnt, and here you are. A full set.
Good morning, people used to say to me, and bow. Now it's the crows, and they don't bow.
It's early for visiting. Early for anything, really, except grudges. Those keep any hour.
Morning. The council will be sitting about now. Somewhere a chair is warm, and it isn't mine.
pariah.greet.evening: Evening. This is when the tavern fills up. I had a seat by the hearth once. They'll have given it to someone duller.
You've come at supper. I'm not sharing. Well. Perhaps a crust.
The sun's going down over {village}. Best view I have of the place. From a distance.
Evening. The lanterns are lit down there. I can count them from here. I do, most nights.
Come to watch the sunset with the outcast? There are worse seats, I suppose. Not many.
pariah.greet.night: It's dark, {player}. Decent folk are abed. So what does that make us?
At this hour? Either you're in trouble or you're trouble. Come in before the zombies decide which.
Night callers. In {village} that meant bad news. Out here it means nothing at all, which is worse.
Couldn't sleep either? Don't look so surprised. Even outcasts have that much in common with people.
Shut the door quickly. Things walk about at night, and only some of them are honest.
pariah.weather.rain: Rain again. It comes in through the cracked window and I let it. We understand each other.
Wet weather. At least nobody expects me at market in this.
Listen to it on the roof. The only thing that visits me without being asked.
Rain washes {village} clean, they used to say. It hasn't managed yet.
Rain's good for the garden. The weeds, mostly. They're the only things that thrive up here.
pariah.weather.thunder: Thunder. The sky shouting at everyone at once. I used to do that in council. Very satisfying.
Let it storm. This house has stood worse. So have I.
Hear that? That's the only applause I get these days.
A storm like this, the whole of {village} will be huddled together. I'll be huddled with myself. Better company.
pariah.weather.snow: Snow. Everything looks clean and forgiven. Don't be fooled.
Snowed in again. As if I needed another excuse to see nobody.
My first winter out here, someone left firewood at my gate. I never found out who. I never thanked them. Snow always reminds me.
Snow on the fence posts. It hides the rot nicely. I could use a coat of it myself.
pariah.weather.clearing: Rain's stopped. The world goes back to pretending it never cried.
There. The sky's done sulking. I could learn from it, I'm told. I won't.
Clearing up. The puddles show the house upside down. It looks better that way.
pariah.weather.hot: Hot enough to wilt a council. Not that mine needed much help.
This heat. The garden's sulking, the well's low and I'm in no mood. Nothing new, then.
Too hot to hold a grudge. Almost. I'm managing.
pariah.chat: I fixed the shutter today. Nobody will see it. That's rather the point.
People in {village} think I sit up here plotting. I sit up here darning socks. Plotting takes company.
I grow my own beans, draw my own water and keep my own counsel. Nobody votes on any of it.
Do you know what I like about living alone? Nobody changes their mind about me overnight.
The house was handsome once. So was I. We've both settled into character.
I talk to the chickens now. They're better listeners than a council, and they've never once voted.
Pity is a cheap coin. Spend it somewhere else.
I keep the good chair for guests. Nobody has ever sat in it. You won't either.
They think I'm lonely out here. I'm not lonely. I'm selective. There's a difference, and I've made it my life's work.
The fence is sagging. I'll fix it when I feel like keeping visitors out properly.
You're bold, walking up to {place} like it's an inn. I almost admire it.
I've counted the cracks in the window. Four. One for each person who ought to have spoken up.
Some days I don't speak a single word. Then you come along and I find I've saved up a few hundred.
Self-sufficient. That's the word. Not abandoned. Self-sufficient. Write it down if you must remember something.
Everyone in {village} has an opinion of me. Not one of them has had the courage to bring it up the hill.
I baked bread this morning. It came out flat and bitter. Like a portrait of the baker.
The garden's gone wild. I let it. Somebody around here ought to do as they please without a vote.
I could go back, you know. Walk right down the high street. I won't, but I could.
People mistake my manners for sorrow. They're just manners. Sharpened.
What do I do all day? I outlast people. It's slow work, but steady.
I mended my coat at the elbows. Twice. I'll mend it again. Everything here gets a second chance except me.
They say I keep to myself. Somebody has to. Nobody else would have me.
A traveller once asked me the way to {village}. I gave it. The right way, even. I'm quite proud of my restraint.
You're very persistent. It's either a virtue or a sickness. I've not decided.
Don't tell anyone in {village} you've been here. Or do. Watch them go pale. That would be worth something.
Out here, a day is just a day. No market, no feast, no seat to defend. It's restful, in a dreadful sort of way.
I chopped enough firewood for two winters. I'm not expecting company. I'm just very angry at logs.
Once, people bowed when I passed. Now the sheep don't even look up.
The roof leaks over the good bed, so I sleep in the bad one. There's a lesson in that I refuse to learn.
If you've come to do good, do it quietly and somewhere else.
I don't need anything. I've told the wind, I've told the crows, and now I'm telling you.
A peddler comes by twice a year and overcharges me for salt. It's the closest thing I have to a friendship.
You don't flinch when I'm rude. That's either kindness or foolishness. Both are rare up here.
I polished the brass on the door. Old habits. A councillor's door should shine, even when the councillor doesn't.
People say this house is going to seed. So is everyone in {village}. They just have more chairs to hide it under.
I read the same three books, over and over. Not one of them has ever turned against me.
The quiet up here isn't empty. It's full of things I'd say if anyone were worth saying them to.
They wanted me gone. I went. That's more obedience than they ever got from me in council.
There's a cat who visits. Not mine. Nobody's. We respect each other's independence.
I've weeded half the garden. The other half has earned the right to stay.
You keep calling it lonely out here. I call it uninterrupted. Well, I did, until you started walking up my path.
On market days I watch the carts go down the far road. I knew every driver by name once. One of them still waves. Badly.
