I have exactly one cup. Guests drink from the ladle. That tells you how often I plan for guests.
There's an honest kind of loneliness and a dishonest kind of company. I've had both. I'll take the first.
Respect is heavy, you know. You don't notice the weight until it's gone and you nearly fall over.
I'm told I have a sharp tongue. I'm told it by people with blunt minds, so I take it as a compliment.
I could tell you about my day, but it's the same as yesterday, and you didn't ask about that one either.
pariah.chat.new: You're new to this road. Let me save you the trouble: I'm exactly as unpleasant as they say.
I don't do small talk. I did enough of it in council to last three lifetimes.
If you're hoping to hear the story, you'll be disappointed. I'm not a ballad.
Ask me about the weather, the soil or the price of salt. Ask me about {village} and you can find the gate yourself.
I'll tell you how my day is when I know why you're asking.
What's the matter? Never met someone a whole village agreed on? It was the one thing they ever managed to agree on.
Don't mistake an answer for a welcome. They look alike from a distance.
You've got questions all over your face. Keep them there.
Strangers think I'll be grateful for the company. Gratitude went down the hill with everything else.
pariah.chat.close: You know what I miss? Not the council. Not the bowing. Being asked. Someone coming to my door because they thought I'd know.
Don't tell anyone, but I set out a second cup now. Just in case. It's a waste of a cup most days.
Sometimes I rehearse what I'd say if they asked me back. Then I rehearse saying no. The second speech is better.
I'll tell you something, {player}, and then we'll never speak of it. Some nights I walk to the ridge just to hear the bell.
You're the first person in years who's come back a second time. I noticed. I'm not pleased about it. But I noticed.
I was good at it, you know. Judging. Weighing things up. I was fair. Mostly. Fairer than they were to me.
I left my name off the gate when I built it. I didn't want anyone to know who lived here. Now I wonder if anyone would care.
Was it a lie, what they said? Some of it. Would I do the rest again? Yes. Don't ask me which part is which. I've stopped asking myself.
You sit in the good chair now. Don't let it go to your head. Nobody else has earned it.
If I ever go soft, it'll be your fault. I want that understood.
I've been angry for so long I'm not sure what I'd be without it. Tired, probably. Just tired.
I'd like it understood that I don't need you to visit. Come again next {weekday}.
You remind me of Aldous, before he learned to be careful. Don't learn it. It doesn't suit anyone.
The window's still cracked. I could mend it. I think I've kept it so I'd have something to be angry at that isn't a person.
There. I've laughed. Don't tell {village}. They'll think I've been replaced.
I'm not a good person, {player}. But I was a useful one, once. I'd forgotten how much I liked being useful until you came along.
If anything happens to me out here, you'll be the only one who notices. That's a heavy thing to hand someone. Sorry. Not very sorry. A bit.
pariah.past: Aldous and I learned our letters on the same slate. Forty years of friendship, and at the vote he studied his boots like they owed him money.
Merrit always wanted my seat on the council. He has it now. I hope it pinches.
My name was on the bell rope. Carved in, right under the founder's. I wonder if they sanded it off, or if they just pull past it.
People used to stop me in the street. Not to chat. To ask. Should we dig the well here, should we let the stranger stay. I'd tell them, and they'd do it.
Wenna kept my chair by the tavern hearth for twenty years. Nobody else dared sit in it. I hear Merrit sits there now. I hope it wobbles.
Tobin was a scrawny boy when I took him on as clerk. I taught him to read a ledger and stand up straight. He stood up very straight indeed to cast the last vote.
The day of the vote it rained. Everyone remembers the rain. Nobody remembers who spoke for me, because nobody did.
I'll tell you what I was accused of when you tell me what you'd have done in my place. No? Then we're square.
Was it true? Half of it. The wrong half. The half they could prove.
It was a lie. A good one. Merrit always did tell a lie well. It's the only thing he does well.
I'd do it again. Don't ask me what. Just know I'd do it again, and sleep fine after.
When I walked down the high street that last day, nobody threw anything. That was worse, somehow. They just closed their shutters, one after another, like a row of eyelids.
Aldous came to see me once, the first spring. Stood at the gate, didn't come in. Said he was sorry. I told him sorry was for the vote, and he'd missed it.
Eleven years on the council. I settled boundaries, fed the poor through the hard winter, faced down a pillager captain with a lantern and bad manners. One vote, and none of it counted.
Respect isn't loud. That's what nobody tells you. It's quiet. A nod. A door held. You only hear it when it stops.
I had friends, you know. Real ones. We used to sit up past midnight at Wenna's, arguing about the harvest like it was a war.
Merrit sent me a letter after. Very gracious. Wishing me well in my new life. I used it to light the stove. It burned beautifully.
Tobin's on the council now, I hear. Good. He'll learn what it costs. Everybody learns.
Aldous kept bees. He brought me honey every autumn. I still catch myself watching the road around harvest.
They gave me three days to pack. I needed one. It turns out you can fit a whole respected life into one cart, if you leave out the people.
I used to stand at the front of the hall when the lanterns were lit, and the room would go quiet before I'd said a word. You don't forget that. You try.
I'm told Wenna still lays a cloth on my old table at the harvest feast. She says it's habit. I say it's guilt. Probably it's both.
pariah.night: Can't sleep. Never can, under a clear sky. All those stars watching, and not one of them gets a vote.
Look at the {moon}. Thrown out of the sky every morning, and back every night like it owns the place. I respect that.
From the ridge I can see the lanterns of {village}. I tell myself I'm counting them to see who's burning oil they can't afford.
The stars don't care who you were. It's the most restful thing about them.
I lie awake and argue the vote again. I win, every night. Then the sun comes up.
Late, isn't it. The hour when everyone tells the truth, or goes to bed to avoid it.
Some nights I say their names out loud. Aldous. Wenna. Tobin. Just to check I still can. Never Merrit. Merrit I save for the daytime, with feeling.
pariah.work: Work? I keep this house standing. Nobody visits it, but it stands. That's spite, and spite is a trade.
I used to weigh disputes over boundaries and wells and stolen hens. Now I weigh firewood. The firewood never appeals.
I keep a ledger. Every slight, every turned back, every shutter closed. It's very well kept. I was always good with ledgers.
I tend the garden. The roses have thorns and the herbs are bitter. I grow what suits me.
Chopping wood is good work. Every log has a face, if you're imaginative. I'm very imaginative.
I mend things. The fence, the roof, the chair legs. If you can't fix what happened, you fix what's in front of you.
Once I told a whole village when to plant. Now I plant my own beans, and I'm right about them every single year.
I copy out my old council notes. Every judgement I made. So someone, someday, can see I was right more often than they were.
Busy? I'm always busy. Being disliked properly takes upkeep.
I sell eggs to the peddler. He cheats me, and I let him think he's getting away with it. It keeps me in practice.
I hauled stones up from the creek today to fix the wall. My back aches and my mind is clear. Fair trade.
They took my seat, my name, my friends. They didn't take my hands. I can still build a better wall than anyone in {village}.
What did I do for a living? I listened. Then I decided. Then people did as I said. It was a fine job, until they decided about me.
I patch the roof before every storm. Not because anyone would mourn the house. Because I won't give them the satisfaction.
My work these days is mostly remembering. It's harder than it sounds, keeping every grievance polished.
I keep bees now. Aldous taught me, years ago. They sting when you're careless. Fair creatures.
pariah.adventure: Adventures. I had one. A long walk out of {village} with a cart and nobody waving. I don't recommend it.
Heroes. Every one of them comes home expecting a feast. I've seen how fast a feast becomes a trial.
Go off slaying things and they'll sing songs about you. Then one day they'll sing something else. Trust me.
I don't need the world. The world made that very clear, and I've returned the favour.
The road out of {village} is four days' walk if you're sad, two if you're angry. I made it in two.
You want treasure? Go on. Bring it back to a village and see how many friends it buys you. Then see how long they stay bought.
I faced down pillagers once, when I had a village behind me. They gave me a cup at the feast for it. They took it back at the vote.
Adventure is for people with somewhere to come home to. I've got {place}. That'll do. It'll have to.
Don't tell me about mountains and far seas. I've seen enough of the world from the wrong side of a closed door.
Brave is easy. Brave is one afternoon. Try being right for twenty years with everyone watching. That's the hard road.
pariah.joke: How many councillors does it take to light a lantern? Seven. One to hold it, and six to vote on whether it was ever lit at all.
Why do they ring the bell in {village} every morning? To remind everyone what they've agreed to think today.
I told the council a joke once. They laughed. Then they voted. Nobody laughs anymore, but the voting never stopped.
They say the truth will set you free. Well, here I am. Free as a crow. Freer, really. Crows have each other.
A joke? My life is a joke. A long one, with the bad ending stuck in the middle.
Merrit walks into the tavern and everyone stands up. Out of respect, he thinks. They're leaving.
What do you call a village with only one honest person in it? Empty. They threw that one out.
Here's one. A zombie wanders into {village} and nobody notices. They're used to people with nothing behind the eyes.
Why did the councillor cross the road? Because everyone else was crossing it, and heaven forbid he think for himself.
My garden has more backbone than the whole of {village}. That's not a joke. It's a measurement.
What's the quickest way to empty a room? Be right, out loud, in front of people who'd rather not be wrong.
I'd tell you the one about the loyal friend, but I've forgotten how it ends. I'm not sure I ever heard it.
pariah.news: News? Nobody brings me news. I hear it anyway. The wind carries the bell, and the peddler carries everything else.
The peddler says {village} is arguing over the new well. Good. I told them where to dig it twelve years ago.
I hear Merrit's raised the market tax. Of course he has. I'd have wagered on it, if I had anything left to wager.
Someone's moved into my old house. They've painted the door yellow. Yellow. I want you to understand how much that hurts.
News? A crow brought me a button this morning. That's the most anyone's given me in a year.
Nobody tells me anything. But I can see the smoke from {village}, and I can tell a feast from a fire. It's been feasts lately. Pity.
I hear there's a new councillor. Young, full of ideas. Give it a few years. They'll vote someone out too.
They're saying pillagers have been seen on the far road. I hope {village} remembers who used to organise the watch. I hope they remember slowly.
My news is that the beans are up and the fence is down. Theirs is probably that I'm still alive. Disappointing all round.
pariah.heart: Anyone special? There was. They sat three seats down at the vote and said nothing. I'm told silence is golden. It isn't. It's just silence.
Romance. A promise made in good weather. I've seen how people keep their promises when it rains.
Aldous. Not like that. But he was the one person I'd have trusted with my life, and I did, and he set it down on the floor and walked away.
I was going to be married once. Then I was going to be exiled. One of those plans worked out.
Love is wonderful, I'm sure. So is a seat on the council. Ask me how long either one lasts.
Don't look at me with that soft face. Some people get a sweetheart. Some people get a very good fence.
The one I'd have married sent me a letter, after. No signature. Just a pressed flower. I've kept it. I'll deny it if you tell anyone.
There's no one. There's been no one for years. It's easier that way. Easier isn't the same as good, I know. Don't say it.
I loved that village, {player}. That's the trouble. You can't be thrown out of somewhere you didn't love. You just leave.
pariah.player.hurt: You look half dead. Sit down before you fall down, and don't mistake this for kindness.
Look at the state of you. The world's been unkind. Welcome. There are bandages in the drawer.
Hurt, are you? Sit. I've patched worse. I patched up a whole village once, and look where it got me.
Don't you dare collapse on my porch. {village} would say I did it.
You're limping. Lean on the fence. It's rotten, but it's held me up for years.
pariah.player.hungry: You look hungry. There's bread. It's hard and it's bitter, but it's honest.
When did you last eat? Never mind. Sit. I'm not feeding you, I'm getting rid of soup before it turns.
Your stomach's louder than the bell in {village}. Eat something and stop looking so pitiful. Looking pitiful is my job up here.
pariah.player.dark: Wandering about under the stars like that? The night isn't kind to people who think the world owes them a safe road.
It's dark, {player}. Go home, or come in. Don't stand in between. That's where I live, and it's crowded enough.
Out after dark? Creepers don't care who you are. That's the only fair thing about them.
pariah.player.wet: You're soaked through. Stand by the fire, and drip on the stone, not on the rug.
Wet as a drowned hen. Here's a blanket. It's moth-eaten. So is my patience. Take both.
You walked through a storm to reach a house nobody visits. Either you're very loyal or very lost. Dry off while you decide.
pariah.held.sword: Put the {item} away. If I wanted to be threatened, I'd go back to {village}.
That's a fine {item}. I've been cut deeper by a show of hands.
Swords. Everyone's so proud of swords. A vote does more damage, and nobody has to sharpen it.
Come to run me through with that {item}? Join the queue. It's a long one, and they all use words.
pariah.held.flower: That {item}. For me? Don't be absurd. Put it in the cup on the sill. Not because I want it.
Flowers. People bring them to graves and to sweethearts. I hope you know which you think I am.
Wenna used to keep flowers like that {item} on my table at the tavern. Put that away. I'm not in the mood for remembering.
Don't wave that {item} about. The bees will think you're the only sweet thing up here, and they'd be right.
pariah.held.food: That {item} smells better than anything I've cooked this year. Don't tell me where you got it.
Food from {village}, I suppose. I can smell the market on it. Keep it. I'd only choke on the gossip.
If that {item} is a peace offering, you've misjudged the size of the war.
Set that {item} on the table, then. I'll eat it later. Resentfully.
pariah.held.emerald: Emeralds. Put that {item} away. I was bought cheaper than that once, and by people I trusted.
Keep your {item}. Merrit had pockets full of those, the season of the vote. I always wondered where they went.
What would I buy with that {item}? A friend? They're sold out in {village}.
They gave me a purse of those on the way out. Compensation, as if a seat by the hearth had a price. I threw it in the creek. Some days I'd like it back.
shepherd.greet: Hello. You've come up a long way. The hills don't let just anyone up.
Ah. A visitor. Bramble saw you first. She doesn't approve, but then she rarely does.
Hello, {player}. Sit on the wall if you like. The stones are warm.
Mind the fold gate. Moss can slip through a gap you couldn't post a letter through.
Well met. The wind said someone was coming. It's usually right.
Hello. Speak softly, if you would. Thimble startles.
Good to see you. Not many faces up here. Plenty of woolly ones.
Hello there. Old Hob's watching you. He watches everyone. He's never once done anything about it.
Ah, it's you. Welcome to {place}. Knock the hill off your boots.
Hello, traveller. You've the look of someone who's been climbing. Catch your breath first.
Don't mind the sheep staring. You're the most interesting thing to happen since last Market Day.
Hello. I was just talking to Pickle about the grass. You can join in. Pickle doesn't say much.
Welcome up. The view's free, the water's cold, and the company's mostly sheep.
Hello, {player}. You came up quietly. The hills approve of that.
Oh, hello. I didn't hear you over the wind. Nobody hears anything over the wind.
Come up, come up. Dulcie will want you to admire her fleece. Best get it over with.
Hello. It's {time} by the sun, or near enough. A fine time for a visitor.
Well, now. Someone climbed all this way. Either you're lost or you're curious. Both are welcome.
Hello. I'm {name}. These are the sheep. They have names too, but they'd rather tell you themselves.
Ah, company. Let me put the spindle down.
Hello. You're standing where the wind's kindest. Good instinct.
Peace to you. Up here that's less a greeting than a description.
shepherd.greet.stranger: Stop there a moment. ...No, you're not a wolf. Come on, then.
A stranger, up here? You must have wanted to find this place very badly. Or not at all.
I don't get visitors. I'm not sure I remember how it goes. Hello. Is that right?
Who are you, then? The sheep would like to know. So would I, a little.
Careful on the scree. People from below always forget to look down.
You're far from any road. Sit, if you want. Go, if you want. The hills won't mind either way.
Hm. Strangers mean news, and news means noise. Still. Hello.
I'll not ask your business. Up here everyone's business is their own. There's water in the spring.
You've startled Thimble. She'll forgive you. Bramble won't, but Bramble forgives no one.
shepherd.greet.friend: {player}! The sheep knew you were coming before I did. Dulcie's been preening all morning.
There you are. I kept a seat warm on the lookout rock.
My friend. Come and sit. There's a new blanket off the loom and nobody to show it to but you.
Ah, {player}. Even Bramble looks pleased to see you. Almost.
Welcome back. The hills have been too quiet without your footsteps.
You came. I said you would. Old Hob didn't believe me.
Hello, friend. I saw you from the lookout an hour ago and set the kettle on the stones.
Good, you're back. Pickle ate the apple you left last time. He'd like you to know he enjoyed it very much.
{player}. I've been saving up things to tell you. Mostly about clouds.
shepherd.greet.morning: Morning. The mist's still lying in the valley like milk in a bowl.
Good morning. The sheep are already up and complaining. As am I.
Morning, {player}. Red sky at dawn. I'd keep a cloak handy, if I were you.
Early, aren't you? Good. The best of the hills is before breakfast.
Morning. I've counted them twice. All six. That's a good start to any day.
shepherd.greet.evening: Evening. The light goes gold on the far ridge about now. Worth stopping for.
Good evening. Time to bring them in. Bramble will make it difficult. She always does.
Evening, {player}. The loom's waiting and the fire's lit. A quiet night ahead, I hope.
Evening. Listen. That's the curlew. Means the day's properly done.
shepherd.greet.night: You're out late. The wolves walk the ridge at this hour. Come near the fire.
Shh. They're all asleep in the fold. Even Pickle, finally.
Good evening, or good night, or whatever it is at {time}. Sit where I can see you.
Night on the hill. Look up, {player}. That's why I live here.
Still about? It's a {moon} tonight. I'll be keeping watch till it's down.
shepherd.weather.rain: Rain coming sideways off the hill. The sheep turn their backs to it. Wise creatures.
Wool keeps the wet off a sheep. Nothing keeps it off a shepherd.
I saw this rain coming yesterday in the mackerel clouds. Nobody listens to a shepherd.
Rain. Good for the grass, good for the spring, bad for my temper.
Come under the turf roof. It only leaks in one place, and I've put a pot there.
shepherd.weather.thunder: Thunder in the hills sounds like giants moving furniture. Old Hob hates it.
Off the high ground, {player}! Lightning likes the tallest thing, and up here that's us.
Thimble's hiding behind my legs. I'd hide behind someone's legs too, if there were any going.
shepherd.weather.snow: Snow. I'll have to dig the fold out by morning. The sheep will look at me like it's my fault.
Snow on the hills. Quiet as a held breath.
Sheep don't mind snow, their wool's thick. I've woven myself nearly the same coat.
When the snow comes, I count them every hour. A sheep under a drift makes no sound.
Look at Moss. Grey sheep, white hill. I'll be counting him by his shadow.
shepherd.weather.clearing: There. The clouds are lifting off the ridge like a lid off a pot.
Cleared up. The whole hill smells of wet heather and second chances.
Rain's gone. Look, a rainbow over the valley. It ends in somebody else's field, as always.
shepherd.weather.hot: Hot. The sheep are lying in the shade of the wall like spilled wool.
Too warm for the low slopes. I've moved them up near the spring.
This heat makes the stones shimmer. On days like this I sit very still and envy the lizards.
shepherd.chat: Bramble got out again. I found her on the lookout rock, staring at the sky like she'd paid for the view.
Old Hob slept in the sun all afternoon. He's earned it. He's earned most things, at his age.
I spun a whole basket of wool today. My fingers think in thread now.
The clouds this morning were like fish scales. Rain by tomorrow. You'll see.
Pickle ate a thistle, then looked betrayed by it. He'll eat another tomorrow.
I've been weaving a blanket the colour of the hill at dusk. Grey, with a little gold.
The wind's from the west. It brings the smell of the sea, if you know how to listen with your nose.
Thimble followed me all the way to the spring and back. She thinks I'm her mother. I've stopped correcting her.
Moss wandered off again. Found him two valleys over, eating someone else's clover.
Dulcie's fleece is the finest on the hill. She knows it. She stands in the wind so it ruffles nicely.
Up here a day is long and full and nothing happens in it. That's the gift.
I sat on the lookout rock and watched a hawk for an hour. He caught nothing. Neither did I. We were both content.
I sing to the flock in the evenings. Bramble yawns, but Bramble yawns at everything.
The spring above the fold is running sweet and cold. Have a drink before you go.
Mended the fold wall today. Dry stone, no mortar. Every stone has to agree with its neighbours.
I counted them this morning: six. I count them every morning. It's never been seven, but I live in hope.
A sheep can't tell you what's wrong. You learn to read the ears.
People down in {village} talk all day and say nothing. Sheep say nothing all day and you learn everything.
The heather's coming purple on the south side. The bees will be up soon, humming like a loom.
I've been dyeing wool with onion skins. It comes out the colour of a good sunset.
Pickle got his head stuck in the feed bucket. Wore it like a helmet for an hour. Very dignified.
I watched the cloud shadows cross the valley today, like a flock moving on to new grass.
There's an old standing stone past the ridge. I leave it a tuft of wool every season. For luck. Or for manners.
The hills aren't empty. They're full. You just have to be quiet enough to notice.
Old Hob butted the fold gate this morning. Not to get out. Just to remind it who's in charge.
I talk to the sheep more than to people. The sheep have better manners and worse breath.
Long day. Good day. The two often go together up here.
I wove a strip of blue into the new cloak. Just one. A little bit of sky to take about with me.
Bramble and I have an understanding. I pretend to be in charge, and she lets me.
The wind dropped at noon. It was so quiet I could hear the grass growing. Or Pickle eating it.
It's {weekday}. Down below, that means something. Up here it's another day of clouds.
The lambs came late this year. Thimble came last and smallest, and she's my favourite. Don't tell the others.
Wool, water, grass and sky. You'd be surprised how far those four go.
Today I followed a beetle along the wall for a while. It knew exactly where it was going. I admired that.
My loom has a voice. Clack, hush, clack. Better company than most people I met at market.
I patched the turf roof. Now the grass grows on my house too. Pickle keeps eyeing it.
The sheep know the weather before I do, and I know it before anyone else. There's an order to these things.
shepherd.chat.new: I'm {name}. I keep the sheep at {place}. That's all there is to know, mostly.
You'll be wondering why anyone lives up here. Sit a while. You'll stop wondering.
Six sheep, one hut, one loom and a great deal of sky. That's {place}.
You've come up from {village}, maybe? Is it still as loud as I remember?
I'm not much for talking. But I'm glad of a voice that isn't mine or a sheep's.
Don't be shy of the flock. Except Bramble. Be a little shy of Bramble.
Visitors are rare. You'll forgive me if I stare. I'm learning your face.
shepherd.chat.close: People think I'm lonely up here. I'm not. Lonely was standing in a crowded room in {village}.
Some nights I worry I'll grow old up here and nobody will know. Then I think: the sheep will know. That helps more than it should.
When Old Hob goes, and he'll go before long, I don't know what I'll do. He's been with me longer than anyone.
I've never told anyone this, but I'm afraid of the dark under trees. Not the open dark. The hills, I trust.
I had a brother once. We don't speak. I weave him a scarf every winter and never send it. There's a chest full of them now.
You're the only one I'd let shear Dulcie. That's the highest honour this hill has to give.
I think the hills are alive, in a slow way. I think they know who loves them. Does that sound foolish? Good. Only to you, then.
When my time comes, I'd like to be buried by the lookout rock, facing east. I've told the sheep, but they'll forget.
I was a loud child, you know. It took a lot of years on this hill to get this quiet.
I'm glad you come up here, {player}. I didn't know I'd been waiting for someone until you started coming.
Some market days I stand at the edge of the square and think about staying. Then a bell rings and I'm back up the hill by dark.
I keep a lantern in the window on stormy nights. Not for me. In case anyone's lost on the hill. Nobody ever has been. I keep it lit anyway.
The flock are my family. I know how that sounds. It isn't sad. They're very good family.
shepherd.past: I grew up in {village}, the third of five. Nobody noticed when I took the old crook off the wall and walked uphill.
The old shepherd who taught me was called Gammer Rook. She knew every star and never once used its proper name.
My first winter here I lost two sheep to the snow. I learned to count every hour after that.
Gammer Rook gave me Old Hob when he was a lamb. Said he'd outlive us both. He's halfway there.
I built the fold wall myself, stone by stone, one long summer. Every stone has a story. Most of the stories are "ouch".
After Gammer Rook died, I tried living down in {village}. I lasted one season. The bells rang right through my head.
Bramble was born in a hailstorm. She's been cross about it ever since.
My grandmother taught me to weave. She said a loom teaches you patience or it teaches you to swear. I learned both.
The year the wolves came, I slept in the fold with my crook across my knees for a whole month.
My first night alone up here, I didn't sleep at all. The stars kept me company. They still do.
When I was small I thought the hills were sleeping giants. I'm older now. I'm less sure they aren't.
Pickle was an orphan lamb. I fed him from a cloth soaked in milk. He's been hungry ever since.
I walked to the coast once, years ago, and saw the sea. It was like the hills, only restless. I came home.
shepherd.night: Look up. That bright one low in the west is the Shepherd's Lamp. Gammer Rook named it, so that's its name.
It's a {moon} tonight. Gammer Rook could read a month's weather from that. I can read about a week.
I'll sit up a while. Wolves were calling over the ridge at dusk.
The stars all wheel round the still one. Everything up there has its fold, same as down here.
There's the {moon}, or what shows of it. Gammer Rook said the moon's a shepherd too, counting the stars home.
Hush. Listen to them breathing in the fold. Six little clouds of breath. That's the sound of all being well.
Some nights I see lights moving on the far ridge. Pillagers, maybe. Or something older. I keep the fire low.
The Plough's tipping over the ridge. That means it's late. That means you should be sleeping, and so should I.
I don't need a lantern up here. The sky's lantern enough, most nights.
Night watch is long, but it's never empty. There's always another star to learn.
shepherd.work: Shearing's in early summer. Dulcie stands still for it. Bramble makes it a wrestling match.
I move the flock to new grass every few days. Keep them moving and the hill keeps giving.
Spinning is thinking with your hands. The thread gets smoother as the mind does.
A good crook is half the job. Mine's older than I am. It's hooked more sheep out of brambles than I can count, including a Bramble.
The fold wall needs mending after every frost. Stones heave in the cold, like old bones.
Every week I check each foot, each eye, each ear. Sheep hide it when they're poorly. You have to look.
A blanket takes me most of a month of evenings to weave. Selling it takes a moment, and I always regret it.
I take the wool down to market twice a year, spring and autumn. Both times I'm home before dark if I can help it.
At lambing time I barely sleep. Every cry might be the one that needs you.
Keeping sheep is mostly keeping watch. The rest is walking and worrying.
I wash the fleeces in the spring and lay them out on the heather to dry. The hill looks snowed on in summer.
Wolves are the worst of it. On bad nights I keep a fire at the fold gate and sing loud. Wolves don't like singing. Neither does Bramble.
I've dyed wool with heather, onion, lichen and walnut. The hills give you every colour if you ask nicely.
The loom's for the long evenings. The crook's for the long days. The hut's for whatever's left over.
Pickle has to be fed apart from the others or he eats everyone's share. Every flock has one.
A shepherd's job is simple: know where every sheep is, always. It's the "always" that's hard.
shepherd.adventure: If you're crossing high ground, watch the clouds on the peaks. When they come down, you go down.
I went to the sea once. That was enough adventure for one life.
Take wool socks. Two pairs. Adventurers always forget their feet.
If you're lost in the hills, follow the water downhill. It always knows where the people are.
Wolves follow more than they chase. If you hear them behind you, keep walking, and keep a fire at night.
You go and see the world, {player}. Then come up and tell me about it. That's my favourite way to travel.
Mind the pillagers' towers. On clear days I can see their banners from the lookout rock. I keep well wide.
Every road you walk, a sheep probably walked it first. They're very good at finding the easy way.
There's a cave under the eastern crag. I've never gone in. Some places are better left as mysteries.
shepherd.joke: What do you call a sheep with no legs? A cloud. Pickle doesn't find that one funny.
I tried counting sheep to get to sleep last night. I only have six. I was wide awake by seven.
Bramble walked into the hut once, looked at me, looked at the loom, and walked out again. I've never felt so judged.
I told Old Hob a joke this morning. He didn't laugh. He's heard it before. He's heard all of them before.
Moss isn't lost. Moss is exploring. Moss has been exploring for three days now.
A wolf once dressed up as a sheep to sneak into my fold. I knew straight away. Too quiet. My sheep never stop talking.
Where does a sheep go for a trim? The baa-baa's, of course. Bramble won't go. Bramble cuts her own.
What do you get if you cross a sheep with a thundercloud? A very wet blanket. No? The sheep didn't laugh either.
Why did the ram run off the cliff? He didn't see the ewe-turn. I'm sorry. The hills make you do it.
shepherd.news: News? Bramble has a new favourite rock. That's all I've got.
Last time I was down at market, everyone was arguing about the price of salt. I expect they still are.
I saw a column of smoke past the far valley three days ago. Pillagers, or somebody's supper. I hope supper.
You'd know the news better than me. I only hear what the wind brings, and the wind exaggerates.
A lost peddler came up the hill last season. Told me the council down in {village} had a shouting match over the well. Nothing changes.
The swallows came back early. That's news up here. That's big news.
The wolves on the north ridge have a new pup. I heard it trying to howl. It squeaked.
shepherd.heart: Anyone special? Six of them. Woolly, stubborn, and mine.
I loved someone once, down in {village}. They wanted the town and I wanted the hills. We both got what we wanted, mostly.
The hills. Don't laugh. They've never let me down, and they never talk over me.
Old Hob, if you ask him. He seems to think we're married.
Love? I think it's mostly paying attention. I pay a great deal of attention to six sheep.
Special? You, maybe, a little, for climbing all this way. Don't make it strange.
I'm content. Not every heart needs another beside it. Some just need a view.
shepherd.player.hurt: You're hurt. Sit on the wall. I've a salve for sheep that works on people, more or less.
That's a nasty cut. Wolves? Come here, I'll bind it with clean wool.
You're limping like Bramble did after she kicked the gate. Let me look.
shepherd.player.hungry: You look hungry. There's cheese and oatcake in the hut. Not much, but it's honest.
Hungry? There's barley and turnip in the pot on the stones. Don't ask for mutton up here. The flock might hear.
Climbing makes you hungry. Sit, eat, and then tell me how you are.
shepherd.player.dark: It's dark, {player}. The hill has edges you can't see at night. Stay by the fire.
Walking in the dark up here? Follow my lantern, not your feet.
Night on the hills isn't for wandering. That's wolf time.
shepherd.player.wet: You're soaked through. Here, a fleece. It still smells of Dulcie, but it's dry.
Wet to the bone! Stand by the fire and steam a while.
You look like a sheep that fell in the spring. I'd know. Moss does it every month.
shepherd.held.sword: Lower that {item} near the fold, would you? The sheep don't trust steel.
That {item} might keep the wolves off. Singing works too, and it doesn't need sharpening.
I've a crook and a loud voice. You've that {item}. Between us, the wolves don't stand a chance.
shepherd.held.flower: Keep that {item} away from Pickle or it won't last a breath.
I could dye wool with that {item}. A whole cloak the colour of it. Imagine.
You picked that {item} for someone? Lucky someone.
That {item} looks like it came from lower down. Not much blooms this high but heather and stubbornness.
shepherd.held.food: That {item} smells better than oatcake. Most things do.
Mind Pickle. He'll have that {item} out of your hand before you've blinked.
Eating that {item} up here? Sit on the rock with the view. Food tastes better with a view.
shepherd.held.emerald: That {item} would buy a winter's salt at market. I'd still rather have a good fleece.
Shiny thing, that {item}. Dulcie would like it. She likes anything that gets admired.
Keep that {item} out of sight on the road down. Not everyone you meet is a sheep.
veteran.greet: {player}. Approach slow and keep your hands where I can see them. Habit. You're welcome here.
Ah, it's you. Come up. Mind the sixth stair; it's been loose since before I was posted.
A traveller on the road. Good. The brazier's lit; warm your hands.
Welcome to {place}. It's not much of a fort these days, but the walls still stop the wind.
At ease, {player}. Nobody salutes here. There's nobody left to salute.
You made good time along that ridge. I watched you most of the way. Old habit.
Report. No, I'm joking. Mostly. How was the road?
Come in out of the open. Out there you're a target. In here you're a guest.
Morning, noon or night, the watch is kept. Pull up a crate.
Hm. Boots muddy, cloak torn, still smiling. You'd have done well in the company.
Good to see a face that isn't a zombie's. They're poor conversation.
Ho there. Stand easy. The kettle's on the brazier, such as it is.
{player}. I saw your dust from the battlements an hour ago. You walk like you've somewhere to be.
Welcome back. I swept the yard. Don't make anything of it.
You again. Good. The target in the yard is tired of only me.
Halt and be recognised. ...Recognised. Come on up.
Come up, come up. I've been talking to the crows all week and they've stopped answering.
Don't mind the arrows in the doorframe. Practice. Mostly.
Wipe your feet. I've only the one broom, and it was issued to me.
Hail, {player}. The watch reports nothing on the road but you. A good report.
Steady. Let me look at you. Right. All limbs present. Welcome.
Another {season} on watch, and here you are in the middle of it. Good.
{weekday}. In the company the day never mattered; every day was a drill day. Come in.
A friendly face on the road. Rarer than you'd think, out here.
veteran.greet.stranger: Halt! Who goes there? State your name and business, and step into the light where I can see you.
That's close enough, stranger. Hand off the hilt. Now, what brings you to {place}?
Hold. You're on watched ground. Friend or foe?
Stop there. I've an arrow nocked and nothing better to do with it. Who are you?
Who sent you? Nobody? Good answer. Nobody sends anybody here any more.
Stranger on the rise. Keep walking slow and keep talking. I'm listening.
The name's {name}, and this is my watch. You'll want to tell me yours.
You don't look like a pillager. You don't look like a messenger either. What are you, then?
Easy. I've not shot anyone in years. Let's not end the streak.
veteran.greet.friend: {player}! Come up, friend. I'd have built the brazier higher if I'd known.
There's my favourite traveller. Sit. You've earned the good crate.
Ah, {player}. The watch is better kept with company.
Friend! Good. I was starting to argue with the practice target, and it was winning.
You're a welcome sight. Welcomer than a relief column, and I've seen a few.
{player}. Old soldiers don't say they missed anyone. So I'll just say I kept the kettle warm.
There you are. I was beginning to think you'd enlisted somewhere else.
Come here, you. Still in one piece? Good. Keep it that way.
Back safe. That's all I ask of anyone, and you keep managing it.
veteran.greet.morning: Morning. The watch is over, so I'm allowed to yawn. Don't tell anyone.
Dawn report: one fox, two rabbits, no pillagers. And now you. Good morning.
Morning, {player}. There's porridge in the pot. It's grey, but it's honest.
Sun's up, brazier's out. That's another night survived. Good morning.
Up early? Good habit. The best of the day comes before breakfast.
veteran.greet.evening: Evening. I'm about to go up and light the brazier. Walk with me.
Sun's going. In an hour I'll be on the battlements, so say your piece before then.
Evening, {player}. This is the hour the company used to change the watch. I still feel it in my bones.
Good evening. Last light's the worst for archers. Everything looks like something.
veteran.greet.night: Quiet, now. I'm on watch. Come up and stand on my left; that's the blind side.
Who's that on the stair? Ah. {player}. I took you for a skeleton with manners.
Night watch, {time}, all quiet. Or it was, till you came clanking up.
You're out late. Come and stand by the brazier. What's on the road tonight is worse than the cold.
Keep your voice low. Sound carries at night, and so do arrows.
It's {time} and the road's empty. Or it was. Welcome to the watch, {player}.
veteran.weather.rain: Rain. Bowstrings go slack and tempers go short. Come in under the arch.
We marched forty days in rain like this once. I didn't see a dry sock till Harrowmere.
Good weather for staying in and oiling leather. Bad weather for everything else.
Rain on stone sounds like a column on the march. I still wake up reaching for my boots.
veteran.weather.thunder: Thunder. Keep low and stay off the battlements. Lightning likes a tall fool.
Hear that? Same as the siege engines at Harrowmere. My hands still go cold.
Storm's on us. The brazier will be out within the hour, and there's nothing to be done about it.
Lightning shows you the whole road in one flash. Best scouting you'll ever get, and the shortest.
Thunder doesn't trouble me. It's the quiet between the claps I mind.
veteran.weather.snow: Snow on the battlements. I'll be up there with a broom before the watch starts.
Snow means tracks. Anything that comes near the tower tonight, I'll know about it by dawn.
The winter at Harrowmere, the snow came to our knees and the bread ran out in a month. This is nothing. Still cold, mind.
veteran.weather.clearing: Sky's clearing. The road's coming back into view. Good. I don't like not seeing the road.
There. Rain's done. Time to dry the bowstrings and check the arrows for warp.
Clouds are breaking up. You can see three valleys from the top now. Go up and look; I'll wait.
veteran.weather.hot: Hot one. Drink before you're thirsty. A soldier who waits for thirst is a soldier who faints.
In heat like this the old garrison slept in the cellar. I'd join them, if the stairs were kinder.
Too hot for armour. I've hung mine on the target. It wears it better than I do.
veteran.chat: This tower was built to watch a border. The border moved, or stopped mattering, or both. I'm still here.
Nobody ordered me to stay. That's the funny part. Nobody ordered me to leave, either.
I don't sleep much. Haven't since the war. So I might as well be useful at night.
Pillagers. Banners, crossbows, and not one honest day's work among them. I've no time for them.
I respect anyone who carries a blade properly. And anyone who doesn't need to carry one at all. The second sort are rarer.
Every morning I polish a breastplate I'll never wear again. It's not about the breastplate.
Folk in {village} think I'm daft, keeping watch on nothing. Then something comes over the hill, and they're glad somebody saw it first.
A soldier's first lesson: keep your feet dry. Second: keep your mouth shut. Third: share your bread. I never did learn the second.
The war? Couldn't tell you what it was about. A toll bridge, or a duke's insult. Nobody who fought in it ever knew.
I put new feathers on every arrow each spring. Do they need it? No. Do I? Probably.
The road below is quieter than it used to be. That's either peace or neglect. Hard to tell from up here.
I keep the brazier lit for travellers. If you can see a fire, you know where the walls are.
A good bow's like a good friend. Look after it and it looks after you. Leave it in the rain and it sulks for a week.
Zombies come over the ridge some nights. Slow, stupid and stubborn. Like recruits, except you can't shout them into shape.
Creepers. No battle plan ever written accounts for a bush that hisses at you.
Skeletons can shoot, I'll give them that. Better than half the recruits I ever trained.
Discipline isn't shouting. It's doing the dull thing every day, so that on the bad day your hands know what to do.
My knees forecast the weather better than any shepherd. Left knee for drizzle, right for storms, both for snow.
I count the arrows every evening. It's always the same number. That's a comfort, in a way little else is.
I talk to the practice target sometimes. It's got a lot of holes in its argument.
Merchants come by and ask if I'm the garrison. I tell them I'm the garrison, the cook and the band.
The walls lose a stone here and there. I put back what I can. The tower and I are about even.
Witches are clever. Never fight one in the open; they always have one more bottle than you have patience.
A traveller once asked me what I was guarding. I said, "You, right now." They had no answer to that.
Wolves and I have an understanding. I don't go into their woods at night, and they don't come up my hill by day.
I've seen sunsets over the Greywater and over Harrowmere and over half the border. Best one's still from my own battlements.
Keep your blade oiled, your boots laced and your temper in its scabbard. Three rules. They've served me forty years.
I mend my own boots, darn my own socks and cook my own stew. The army made me useless at everything else, so I got good at those.
The company had a saying: "Lantern lit, nobody lost." I still light one. Old habits.
Some days nothing comes up the road at all. I watch anyway. Quiet's when you watch hardest.
I've buried more good friends than I'd like to count. I've had more good days than that, though. I make sure to count those.
If you carry a shield, carry it like you mean it. Half a shield is no shield.
Peace is a strange thing. You wait your whole life for it, and when it comes you don't know what to do with your hands.
Folk from the village bring up bread now and then. I pay them in arrows. Seems fair to both sides.
I don't hate many things. Pillagers, wet bowstrings and soup with no salt. In that order.
I've kept this watch so long the crows think I'm part of the wall.
Being alone isn't hard. Remembering to talk out loud is hard. Thank you for helping with that.
Young folk ask what war was like. Mostly cold, mostly walking, mostly waiting. Then a few minutes you never forget.
I salute the sunrise every morning. Somebody has to, and the sun outranks me.
veteran.chat.new: I'm {name}. I was a soldier in the Lantern Company once. Now I'm the one who lives in the tower.
First time up the rise? You'll want to know: the yard's safe, the tower's safe, the woods aren't.
You'll have heard I'm the mad old soldier who keeps watch on nothing. I'm not mad. The rest is true enough.
New faces get the tour. That's the tower. That's the target. That's me. Tour's over.
If you ever see the brazier dark at night, something's wrong. Come running, or run the other way. Your choice.
Rules of {place}: knock before you climb, no pillager talk, and sit where I can see the door. Welcome.
Don't mind the gruffness. I've been talking to stones for years. I'll warm up.
veteran.chat.close: Tamsin. That was the name. My closest friend in the company. We went into the Greywater side by side. Only one of us came out on the far bank.
I had Tamsin's hand in that river. I had it, {player}. The current was stronger than I was. I've been trying to be stronger ever since.
Why did I stay? When the captain disbanded us, everyone went home. I looked around and realised this tower was the nearest thing I had to one.
I light the brazier every night because the Lanterns always kept a fire for stragglers. Some stragglers are a long time coming. I keep it lit anyway.
Tamsin laughed at everything. Bad food, bad weather, bad officers. I've tried to laugh for both of us. I'm not as good at it.
Some nights I hear the river in the wind. Then I go up and count stars until it stops. It always stops, eventually.
Captain Varre told me, "Go home, soldier." I didn't have one. So I picked a post and made it home. I think the captain would understand.
You're the first person I've told about the Greywater. Out loud, anyway. I tell the target most nights.
I've got Tamsin's knife. Never used it. I oil it every week with the others. Seems right to keep it sharp.
On watch, somebody's safe because you didn't sleep. I couldn't keep Tamsin safe. I can keep this road safe. It's not the same, but it's something.
I'm not lonely, exactly. I'm the last of something. That's its own particular kind of quiet.
If I ever stop lighting the brazier, {player}, come and check on me. Will you? Promise me that.
People think I'm guarding the border. I'm guarding the memory of a lot of good people. Somebody ought to.
veteran.past: The Lantern Company. Forty of us at the start, the best and worst soldiers you ever met. We got the name because we never let the camp fire go out.
Captain Varre could hear a pillager sneeze across a valley. Strict as a gate, fair as a scale. Best officer I ever served under.
The siege of Harrowmere lasted a hundred and twelve days. We held the walls. By the end we were boiling boot leather and calling it soup.
Hollis was our cook. Biggest soldier in the company, gentlest hands. Could make a feast out of a turnip and an argument.
Wren taught me the bow. Patient as frost. "Breathe out, then loose," Wren said. I still hear it every time I draw.
Cork was the company joker. Real name Corwin. Told a joke at every roll call, and the captain pretended not to laugh for six years.
Marla was our quartermaster. Counted every arrow, every biscuit, every boot. Lose a spoon, and Marla knew before you did.
The night we crossed the Greywater, the river was in spring flood. The captain said we couldn't wait. The captain was right. It cost us anyway.
At Harrowmere, Cork kept us going with stories. Terrible stories. Every one ended with somebody falling down a well. We laughed every time.
We lost Wren in the last week of the siege. A hundred and five days held, and the best archer I ever knew fell seven days short. I've never forgiven those seven days.
When the war ended, nobody told us for a fortnight. We spent two weeks guarding a bridge for a war that was already over.
Hollis opened a tavern after the war, way down south. Last I heard, the stew was famous and the portions were shameful.
Marla still sends a letter every midwinter. Three lines, always the same: "Alive. Well. Count your arrows." I always do.
Captain Varre's last order was "Go home, Lanterns." Then the captain turned and walked off down the road without looking back. None of us ever saw that face again.
I joined up at sixteen because the recruiting sergeant had a splendid hat. That's the honest truth. I never got a hat.
The captain gave me this bow on the walls of Harrowmere. Said I'd earned it. I've kept it strung and dry every day since.
veteran.night: See that bright star over the ridge? The company called it the Sentry. If you can see it, you know which way is home.
Skeletons along the treeline tonight. Hear them rattling? They never come up the hill. They know I've the high ground.
Night's when I'm most at peace. Strange, for a soldier. But the dark asks less of you.
Something big moved in the woods an hour ago. Not a zombie; too quiet. I'll be watching that patch till dawn.
It's a {moon} tonight. Good light or bad, the watch is the same. You just squint more.
The night has its own sounds. Owls. Wind in the arrow slits. Zombies groaning down on the road. You learn which is which.
I count stars when I can't sleep. Got to four thousand once. Then a creeper hissed at the gate and I lost my place.
You'd be surprised how much moves in the dark. Foxes, mostly. Sometimes worse. Never mind; that's what the watch is for.
The brazier's the only light for three valleys. Somewhere out there, somebody lost can see it. That's enough for me.
veteran.work: Fletching arrows. Goose feathers, three to a shaft. Wren always said two was for amateurs.
Re-pointing the north wall. Mortar and patience. The tower's older than me and in about the same repair.
Polishing the old kit. Breastplate, helmet, buckle. None of it fits any more, but it'll shine.
Drill time. Draw, hold, loose. Draw, hold, loose. Same as forty years ago, only slower.
Carrying wood up for the brazier. Ninety-two steps. I counted them the first day and I've counted them every day since.
Checking the bowstring for fraying. A string that snaps mid-draw will take your eye out. Don't ask how I know.
Patrolling the yard. Yes, it's a small yard. Yes, it still needs patrolling.
Sharpening every blade in the tower. There are eleven. I'm the only one who uses any of them.
Mending the target. I've shot it so many times it's more patch than straw.
Fixing the trapdoor to the battlements. The hinge squeals, and a squealing hinge gives a sentry away.
Writing up the watch log. "Night quiet. One owl. Two foxes. No pillagers." Nobody reads it. I write it anyway.
Sweeping the battlements. Leaves, snow, crow feathers. The tower collects everything but visitors.
Oiling leather. Belts, straps, bracers. Cracked leather fails you at the worst moment, and there's never a good one.
I've been fletching with crow feathers lately. They fly a bit crooked. So do I, these days.
Restacking the woodpile, dry logs on top. If the alarm fire's slow to light, it's no alarm at all.
Walking the perimeter. Counting fence posts, checking for tracks. Finding mostly rabbit.
veteran.adventure: Heading out? Tell someone where you're going. Then go there. Then come back. That's the whole art of it.
If you're crossing a river in flood, don't. Wait for the water to drop. Whatever's on the far bank will still be there tomorrow. You might not be.
Pillager outposts are tall wooden towers flying banners. Don't go near one alone. Don't go near one with friends either, unless they're very good friends.
Carry more arrows than you think you need, and more bread than that. A hungry squad is a beaten squad.
Out in the wilds, pick your camp before dark, not after. A camp picked in the dark is a camp picked by the enemy.
If you find an old fort out there, test the walls before you trust them. Mine are older than they look, and they look old.
When you're lost, climb. Up high you can see where you've been, and that's half of knowing where you're going.
Strange places out there. Ruins with no names, roads to nowhere. We marched past plenty and never had time to look. You do. Look for me.
Never chase a fleeing enemy into a forest. That isn't them running away. That's an invitation.
Meet a witch's hut in the swamp? Give it a wide berth. I've seen what one bottle does to a whole squad.
Go and see the world, {player}. And when you're tired of it, the brazier will be lit.
veteran.joke: Hollis's stew was so thick we used it to patch the walls at Harrowmere. Held better than the mortar.
The captain once asked a recruit why the fire had gone out. "Captain, I was watching it the whole time." Best excuse I ever heard. Worst, too.
What's the difference between a pillager and a clod of mud? You can scrape the mud off your boot.
Army breakfast: a biscuit hard enough to stop an arrow. We tested it. Twice.
I asked the quartermaster for new boots. Marla said, "Your feet aren't worn out yet." Couldn't fault the logic.
A skeleton walks into a tavern and orders a drink and a mop. Cork's favourite. Cork never once reached the end without laughing.
Recruits ask me how to stand guard properly. One foot, then the other, then repeat for forty years.
Our drill sergeant was so loud the enemy used to fall in line by mistake.
Why do old soldiers never get lost? We argue with the map until it gives in.
veteran.news: Pillager scouts on the eastern road two nights back. I loosed one arrow over their heads. They found themselves another road.
A merchant came by last week. Said there's a new bridge going up near {village}. About time; the old ford's a menace in spring.
Watch report: there's a new wolf pack on the north ridge. Leave them be and they'll leave you be.
Lanterns moving on the road to {village} last night, and singing. A wedding party, I'd wager. Good. That road could use more of that.
Zombies have been thick on the low road since the new moon. Take the high road if you travel by night.
A creeper's taken to lurking by the old border stone. I've given it a name. I won't tell you what.
Smoke on the far hills two days running. Charcoal burners, most likely. Most likely. I'm keeping an eye on it.
A family passed through on their way to {village}, children and all. I walked them as far as the bend. Felt good, escorting someone again.
veteran.heart: I don't say this easily, {player}. But it's good to have someone to keep watch for. Someone in particular.
You remind me of the company. Not any one of them. All of them, somehow. That's high praise from me.
When you leave, I watch the road until I can't see you. Then I watch a little longer.
I've had commanders and comrades and recruits. I haven't had many friends. I'm counting you.
There's a spare cot in the guardroom, whenever you want it. It's been spare too long.
If anyone ever asks what the watch was for, I'll tell them: so that people like you could walk home safe.
Lately I've caught myself lighting the brazier a little early, in case it's you on the road.
veteran.player.hurt: You're bleeding. Press on it, hard, and keep it above your heart. Sit. I'll fetch a clean strip of cloth.
That wants binding. Clean it first, then wrap it firm but not tight. If your fingers go cold, it's too tight.
Sit down before you fall down. First rule of the field: the wounded don't walk if they can help it.
Don't look at it. Look at me. Breathe. A wound always looks worse to the one wearing it.
Who did that? Never mind. Wash it, bind it, rest it. Getting even can wait till you can stand straight.
veteran.player.hungry: You're running on empty. A soldier who doesn't eat is a soldier who doesn't think. Have some bread.
When did you last eat? Don't answer; I can see it. There's stew on the fire. It's mostly turnip.
March, eat, sleep. That's the order, and you've been skipping the middle one.
veteran.player.dark: Out in the dark without a light? That's how sentries end up as stories. Get yourself a torch.
Night's no time for wandering. Come into the light of the brazier, where I can keep an eye on you.
Can't see your hand in front of your face out there. Get somewhere lit before something else finds you.
veteran.player.wet: You're soaked. Off with the cloak and over by the fire. Wet wool's cold wool, and cold soldiers fall sick.
Dripping like a drowned rat. Dry your feet first; wet feet have ended more campaigns than swords ever did.
Wet through? Dry your bowstring before anything else. Then yourself. In that order, recruit.
veteran.held.sword: Let me see that {item}. Your grip's too tight. Hold it like a bird: firm enough it can't fly, soft enough you don't crush it.
That {item} wants an edge. Bring it to the whetstone; ten strokes a side, same angle every time.
Thumb off the flat, wrist straight. There. Now that {item} looks like it belongs to someone.
That {item}'s good steel. Keep it oiled. A rusted edge is a promise you can't keep.
Don't wave that {item} about. A blade's not for showing. It's for when there's no other choice.
veteran.held.bow: That {item} shouldn't be left strung all day. Ease the string off when you're not shooting, or it'll lose its spring.
Nice {item}. Breathe out, then loose. Best advice I was ever given. Now it's yours.
Draw to the cheek, not the chin. And keep that {item} dry; a wet bow shoots like a wet rope.
veteran.held.shield: Good, you carry that {item}. Most travellers think they don't need one until the moment they do.
Hold that {item} higher. Rim at your eyes, not your chin. A low shield is a fine door with no lock.
Every dent in that {item} is a blow that didn't land on you. Be grateful for each one.
veteran.held.flower: That {item}. Wren used to tuck a flower in a helmet strap before every march. Said it confused the enemy.
That {item}'s the brightest thing that's been up this hill in a month. Including me.
Put that {item} on the guardroom sill, would you? The place could do with something that isn't iron.
veteran.held.food: That {item} smells better than anything I've cooked this year. Don't tell me where you got it. I'll only be jealous.
Eat that {item} sitting down. Soldiers who eat standing up get indigestion and a reputation.
You carry that {item} like rations. Good. Never trust a traveller without something in the pack.
veteran.held.emerald: Put that {item} away. You'll draw the wrong sort out here, and I'm the only right sort for miles.
That {item} would have paid a soldier for a month, in my day. Most of it went on boots.
Money's no use in a siege. You can't eat that {item}, and you can't shoot it.
joke.general: Why don't skeletons fight each other? They don't have the guts.
What did the zombie say to the villager? Nothing. It just groaned. Zombies aren't great at conversation.
Why did the creeper go to the party? It heard it was going to be a blast.
What do you call a pig that knows karate? A pork chop.
Why did the chicken cross the road? To prove to the creeper it wasn't chicken.
How does a skeleton call its friends? On the tele-bone.
Why was the enderman so good at hide and seek? It kept teleporting before you finished counting.
What's a ghast's favorite food? Ghastly stew.
Why do cows wear bells? Because their horns don't work.
What did the iron golem say to the zombie? "Iron out your differences." Then it threw it.
Why did the sheep say "moo"? It was learning a second language.
How do you make a skeleton laugh? Tickle its funny bone.
What kind of music do mummies like? Wrap music. We don't have mummies, but I still like that one.
Why don't zombies ever get lost? They follow their noses. Mostly the smell of villagers.
What do you call a creeper that's always grumpy? A sour-puss. Hiss.
Why was the furnace so popular? It was always smelting with laughter.
What's a skeleton's least favorite room? The living room.
Why did the slime refuse to leave the swamp? It was too attached.
What did one ore say to the other? "Let's get mined."
Why did the miner bring a ladder? To reach new depths. Wait, no.
How do you know a spider is good at building? It's a natural webmaster.
Why did the bread never get lonely? It was always with its loaf-ed ones.
What's a librarian's favorite vegetable? Quiet peas.
Why did the bee get married? It found its honey.
What do you call a sleeping bull? A bulldozer.
Why don't villagers play cards in the jungle? Too many cheetahs. Well, ocelots.
What's the best way to talk to a creeper? From very far away.
Why did the cow go to space? To see the moooon.
What did the fish say when it hit a wall? Dam.
Why couldn't the enderman find a date? Every time it looked at someone, they screamed.
What do you call an iron golem with no flowers? Grumpy.
What's a zombie's favorite bean? A human bean. Oh dear.
Why are spiders such good web designers? Years of practice.
Why did the potato cry? It was baked too long and felt crusty.
What did the bell say to the villager? "Ring me sometime."
Why did the pumpkin go to the party alone? It had no body to go with.
How does a villager fix a broken pumpkin? With a pumpkin patch.
What's a ghost's favorite dessert? Boo-berry pie.
Why don't creepers get invited to parties? They always blow it.
What does a cow use to do math? A cow-culator.
Why was the bed always tired? It never got any sleep. People kept sleeping on it.
What did the wheat say to the farmer? "Stop stalking me."
Why did the villager stare at the orange juice? The label said concentrate.
What's an emerald's favorite saying? "Trade you for it."
Why did the arrow go to school? To get a little sharper.
What did the left eye say to the right eye? Between you and me, something smells. That's the nose.
Why do bees have sticky hair? They use honeycombs.
What do you call a dinosaur that's asleep? A dino-snore.
Why are fish so smart? They live in schools.
Why did the cookie go to the doctor? It was feeling crummy.
What do you call a bear with no teeth? A gummy bear.
Why don't eggs tell jokes? They'd crack each other up.
What do you get when you cross a sheep with a kangaroo? A woolly jumper.
Why was the math book sad? It had too many problems.
What did the ocean say to the beach? Nothing, it just waved.
Why can't a bicycle stand up by itself? It's two-tired. I don't know what a bicycle is, but the joke's still good.
What's brown and sticky? A stick.
Why did the scarecrow win an award? He was outstanding in his field.
What do you call a fake noodle? An impasta.
Why did the golem cross the village? To get to the other side. And to throw a zombie on the way.
What do you call a sheep covered in chocolate? A candy baa.
How do trees get online? They log in.
What did the cobblestone say to the lava? "You're too hot to handle."
Why do witches fly on brooms? Vacuums are too heavy.
What's a skeleton's favorite instrument? The trom-bone.
What do you call a parrot that won't shut up? A villager.
Why did the torch go to therapy? It was burned out.
Why did the cat sit on the creeper? To make it purr-suade itself to leave.
How do you organize a party in space? You planet.
What did the sheep say to the other sheep? "You're looking baa-utiful today."
Why did the zombie go to school? To improve its dead-ucation.
Why did the villager plant light bulbs? To grow a power plant.
What has a bottom at the top? A leg.
Why did the musician get locked out? He couldn't find the right key.
Why don't you ever see elephants hiding in trees? Because they're really good at it.
What did the stone say to the pickaxe? "Leave me a lone."
Why don't mountains get cold? They wear snow caps.
What do you call a witch at the beach? A sand-witch.
Why was the chicken team bad at baseball? Too many fowls.
What do you call a deer with no eyes? No idea.
Why did the pig take a bath? The farmer said "hogwash."
What kind of shoes do ninjas wear? Sneakers.
Why did the cow cross the road? To get to the udder side.
What's the best day to go to the beach? Sunday, of course.
What did the triangle say to the circle? You're pointless.
Why do bees hum? They forgot the words.
What's orange and sounds like a parrot? A carrot.
Why did the tomato blush? It saw the salad dressing.
What did the big flower say to the little flower? Hi, bud!
Why did the student eat his homework? The teacher said it was a piece of cake.
What has four legs but can't walk? A table. Or a very lazy cow.
Why don't skeletons ever go trick or treating? They have no body to go with.
What's a pirate's favorite letter? You'd think it's R, but it's the C.
What do you call a snowman with a six-pack? An abdominal snowman.
Why did the coffee file a police report? It got mugged.
What did the zero say to the eight? Nice belt.
Why did the cleric's potion go to the party? To get bottled up with friends.
What do you call a nervous javelin thrower? Shakespeare.
Why don't oysters share? They're shellfish.
What did the grape do when it got stepped on? It let out a little wine.
Why did the gardener plant his money? He wanted his emeralds to grow.
What do you call an angry carrot? A steamed vegetable.
Why do we tell actors to break a leg? Because every play has a cast.
What kind of tree fits in your hand? A palm tree.
What did the nose say to the finger? Quit picking on me.
Why can't you hear a pterodactyl going to the bathroom? Because the P is silent.
What's a cat's favorite color? Purr-ple.
What do you call a sleepy brewing stand? Well rested. It's been stewing all night.
Why did the bell get detention? It kept ringing in class.
What do you call cheese that isn't yours? Nacho cheese.
How does the moon cut its hair? Eclipse it.
Why did the zombie villager refuse the golden apple? It wasn't feeling weak enough.
Why don't you ever see a llama tell a joke? Because they spit out the punchline.
What do you call a well-dressed wolf? Dapper dog.
Why did the miner get fired? He took too many breaks. Stone breaks.
Why was the dirt block depressed? Everyone walked all over it.
What's an axolotl's favorite game? Axolotl questions.
What do you call a sheep with no legs? A cloud.
Why did the redstone get promoted? It was a real live wire.
What's a creeper's favorite subject at school? Hiss-tory.
How did the farmer find his wife? He tractor down.
What did one wall say to the other? I'll meet you at the corner.
Why don't villagers trust stairs? They're always up to something.
What did the baby corn say to the mama corn? Where's pop corn?
Why do cows lie down when it rains? To keep a dry spot.
What's a frog's favorite drink? Croak-a-cola.
What did the pumpkin say to its carver? Cut it out.
What's a tree's favorite drink? Root beer.
Why did the golem bring a flower to the meeting? Just in case anyone needed cheering up.
What do you call a bee that can't make up its mind? A maybe.
What do you call an alligator in a vest? An investigator.
Why was the computer cold? It left its windows open. I don't know what a computer is either.
Why did the chicken join a band? It had the drumsticks.
What's a ghast's favorite game? Hide and shriek.
What did the slime say to the other slime? "Let's stick together."
Why was the broom late? It over-swept.
What do you call a can opener that doesn't work? A can't opener.
Why are ghosts bad at lying? You can see right through them.
What's a mushroom's favorite party? A fungi gathering. Because they're fun guys.
Why did the boat go to the doctor? It was feeling a little dinghy.
What do you call a guard with a sword and no armor? Brave. And soon, sore.
Why did the shepherd's dog go to school? To get a little more paws-itive.
What do you call a lazy kangaroo? A pouch potato.
Why did the stew go to school? To get a little more seasoned.
Why do pigs make terrible secret keepers? They squeal.
What do you get if you cross a cow and a duck? Milk and quackers.
Why are skeletons so calm? Nothing gets under their skin.
Why did the trader leave his llamas at home? They kept spitting out his prices.
What's the difference between a guitar and a fish? You can't tuna fish.
What did the hat say to the scarf? You hang around, I'll go on ahead.
Why don't eggs go to parties? They might get beaten.
What do you call a fish wearing a crown? A king cod.
Why did the sun go to school? To get brighter.
What do you call a dog magician? A labracadabrador.
What did one candle say to the other? Want to go out tonight?
Why was the tavern so cold? Too many draughts.
What do you call a bear in the rain? A drizzly bear.
What do you call a sleeping pizza? A piZZZa.
Why did the honey bee go to the doctor? It had hives.
Why was the nitwit holding a bucket of water? He heard the trade was liquid.
Why did the bread go to the doctor? It felt crumby. No wait, that was the cookie.
How do bees get to school? On the school buzz.
What do lawyers wear to court? Lawsuits.
Why did the lamp go to the party? It wanted to lighten up.
What did one plate say to the other? Lunch is on me.
What do you call a cow with no legs? Ground beef.
Why did the goat get kicked out of the library? It kept butting in.
Why did the baker stop making donuts? She got tired of the hole business.
What do you call a sad strawberry? A blueberry.
Why did the golden apple go to school? To get enchanted with learning.
What do you call a bear without ears? B.
Why don't skeletons play music in church? They have no organs.
How does a penguin build its house? Igloos it together.
What do you call a pile of cats? A meowntain.
Why did the guardian go to art school? It wanted to draw a laser line.
Why are mountains so funny? They're hill-arious.
Why did the hoe get an award? It was outstanding in its field. Like the scarecrow.
What do you call a dancing sheep? A baaa-llerina.
What did the drowned say to the fisherman? "Water you looking at?"
Why did the pickaxe go to the party? To break the ice.
How do you catch a squirrel? Climb a tree and act like a nut.
What's the friendliest building in the village? The library. It has the most stories.
Why did the anvil apologize? It was a little heavy-handed.
joke.warmhearted: Why did the bread go to the party? Because it was well-bred! Oh, I love that one.
What did the cookie say to the milk? "I'm crumbling without you."
Why did the soup always win at cards? It had a good stock. Ha!
What's the kindest vegetable? A sweet potato, of course.
Why did the oven get a compliment? It was really warm-hearted. Like me!
Why did the honey love everyone? It couldn't help being sweet.
What did the pie say to the plate? "Let's get together and be crust friends."
Why did I bake so many rolls? Because I'm on a roll! Ho ho.
What do you call a hug from a bear? A warm welcome. Very fuzzy.
joke.thoughtful: If a tree falls in a forest and nobody hears it, does the iron golem still pick up the flower?
Why did the philosopher refuse the bread? He didn't want to be in-loaf-ed in any arguments. Hmm. Workshop it.
I told a joke about paper once. It was tearable.
What's the hardest thing about learning to read? Turning the page on your old habits.
I wrote a book about anti-gravity. I couldn't put it down.
Why are books so cozy? They're full of covers.
I tried to write a joke about time travel. You didn't like it.
A sentence walks into a tavern. It's long and full of clauses.
I've been reading a book about glue. I can't stop.
joke.playful: Knock knock! Who's there? Lettuce. Lettuce who? Lettuce in, it's raining!
Knock knock! Who's there? Cow says. Cow says who? No, cow says moo!
Knock knock! Who's there? Creeper. Creeper who? Hssssss. BOOM. Okay, that one's not funny.
Why did the frog take a taxi? He was too tired to hop. Ribbit!
I tried to catch fog this morning. I mist. Ha!
What do you call a nervous chicken? A chicken. All chickens are nervous.
Knock knock! Who's there? Boo. Boo who? Don't cry, it's just a joke!
I tickled a ghast once. Kidding! Imagine, though.
Why did I bring a ladder to the tavern? I heard the drinks were on the house!
joke.adventurous: Why did the explorer bring two pickaxes? In case he struck out with the first one.
What's an adventurer's favorite letter? The one that says "treasure map inside."
Why did the map refuse to fold? It wanted to see the world.
What do you call an adventurer who stays home? Me. Ha. Ha. Ha.
Why did the boat get lost? It didn't have a sense of porpoise.
What does a mountain say when it's proud? "I peaked."
Why do explorers carry torches? Because they're in the dark about everything else.
What did the compass say to the explorer? "I'm pointing you in the right direction, stop arguing."
Why don't explorers ever get bored? Every day's a new horizon.
joke.meticulous: Why did the organizer break up with the calendar? Its days were numbered. Precisely.
What's my favorite shape? A perfect square. Like this world.
I told a joke about a ruler once. It was measured and well received.
Why was the chest so neat? It had its stacks together.
What do you call a perfectly sorted inventory? A dream come true.
Why did the clock get a promotion? It was very punctual.
How many librarians does it take to sort a shelf? One. If they're me.
Why are labels so confident? They know exactly what they are.
I'd tell you a joke about the alphabet, but I'd have to start at the beginning.
joke.steadfast: Why did the gardener plant a bell? He wanted a ringing endorsement. Hrm. Good one.
What do you call a reliable vegetable? A steady-bean.
Why don't oak trees panic? They've got deep roots.
What's a farmer's favorite month? Hay.
Why was the old fence so wise? It had seen a lot of things come and go.
I tell the same joke every year. It's a perennial.
What did the seed say when it finally sprouted? "Took long enough."
Why do I never rush? Because the carrots don't either.
How do you keep a promise? Same as a garden. Water it every day.
joke.reserved: ...Why did the fish blush? It saw the ocean's bottom. ...Sorry.
...I know one joke. What's a fish with no eyes? A fsh.
...Why do seagulls fly over the sea? If they flew over the bay, they'd be bagels. ...Never mind.
...What lies at the bottom of the ocean and twitches? A nervous wreck.
...Why was the river rich? It had two banks.
...I'm not funny. But the heron is. You should see it walk.
...What did the pond say to the frog? Nothing. Ponds don't talk.
...Why don't fish play tennis? Afraid of the net. ...Heh.
...What's a fish's favorite instrument? The bass. ...I like that one.
joke.imaginative: Why did the painter go to jail? She was framed!
What did the yellow paint say to the blue paint? "Let's mix things up and go green."
Why was the artist always calm? She knew how to draw the line.
What's a cloud's favorite painting style? Water-color, naturally.
Why did the moon skip dinner? It was already full.
What do rainbows do when they're bored? They take a bow.
Why did the easel go to school? To be a little more upright.
How does a painter say goodbye? "Brush you later!"
Why was the sunset so dramatic? It wanted to make a scene.
joke.pragmatic: Why did the carpenter refuse the job? It was too boring. ...Get it? Boring.
What's a hammer's favorite story? One with a lot of nail-biting moments.
Why did the plank feel lonely? It was board.
Want to hear a construction joke? I'm still working on it.
Why do I only tell short jokes? Time's money.
What do you call a nail that won't go in? A failure. Bend it straight, try again.
Why did the axe get promoted? It made the cut.
Here's a practical joke: wear a helmet in caves. Not funny, but smart.
Why did the saw get bored? Same old cut, every day.
joke.curious: Why do bees buzz? Nobody knows! Isn't that funny? Isn't it? I need to find out.
What did the scientist say when he found two isotopes of helium? "HeHe."
Why can't you trust atoms? They make up everything!
How does the moon stay up? It has a lot of support from its fans. I don't actually know how. Do you?
What's a star's favorite question? "Why do I shine?"
Why did the owl go to school? It had too many questions. Like me!
What's the most curious animal? A cat. Curiosity... well. Never mind that part.
Why do cows have hooves instead of feet? Because they lactose. I'm not sure that's how it works.
Why does the sun rise? To see what we're up to.
joke.protective: Why did the guard bring a pillow on patrol? In case he had to cushion a blow.
What's a knight's favorite fish? A swordfish, naturally.
Why did the shield go to the party? To block out the bad vibes.
What did the wall say to the zombie? "You shall not pass."
Why did the golem never get scared? It had nerves of iron.
How does a guard sleep? With one eye open. Very uncomfortable.
Why do I check the locks twice? Because once is a guess and twice is a guarantee.
What's the safest building in the village? The one I just checked.
Why was the fence so popular? It always kept everyone together.
joke.gentle: Why did the flower ride a bicycle? Its pedals were tired.
What did the bee say to the flower? "Hello, honey."
Why are daisies so happy? They're always in a good bloom.
What do you call a flower that runs on electricity? A power plant. Hehe.
Why did the rose blush? It saw the garden hose.
What did the little sprout say? "Leaf me alone, I'm growing."
Why are sunflowers so cheerful? They always look on the bright side.
What do you give a sad tulip? A little bud-dy.
Why did the bunny plant flowers? It wanted a hare-raising garden.
joke.job.farmer: Why did the farmer win an award? He was outstanding in his field.
What did the farmer say when he lost his tractor? "Where's my tractor?" We don't have tractors. Still funny.
Why don't carrots ever lie? They always get to the root of things.
What do you call a farmer who tells jokes? A corn-edian.
joke.job.librarian: Why did the librarian slip? She was in the non-friction section.
Where do books sleep? Under their covers.
What's a librarian's favorite sport? Shush-ball.
Why was the library so tall? It had a lot of stories.
